extraction.body: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” [Video: Personal Intelligence in cars] Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

sources.title: Get hands-free personalized help on the road with Gemini - blog.google
passages: Get hands-free personalized help on the road with Gemini
Gemini is now available on Android Auto and cars with Google built-in, offering a hands-free way to manage tasks while driving.
You can now enable Personal Intelligence to let Gemini pull information from your emails, photos, and calendar to provide tailored answers to complex questions.
To get started, check your Gemini settings to opt in and connect your preferred apps.
An assistant is even more helpful when it knows the world and knows you.
With Gemini, you can speak naturally to get more done or brainstorm ideas while driving.
If you've already enabled it in the Gemini app, it comes with you into the car.
You’re in total control of your privacy, so you can choose exactly what information Gemini can access.
We built Personal Intelligence with privacy at the center .
Personal Intelligence has two core strengths: retrieving specific details from, say, an email, photo or a place you saved in Google Maps to answer your question and reasoning across complex sources.

Personal Intelligence is currently rolling out to eligible personal Google accounts (and not for Workspace business, enterprise, or education users) aged 18 and older globally, excluding the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and Nigeria.

An assistant is even more helpful when it knows the world and knows you. That’s why we’re rolling out Personal Intelligence with Gemini starting today, 1 to give you uniquely tailored answers and make Gemini even more valuable on the road. sources.title: Gemini can now draw on your Google data to personalize the images it generates - Engadget
passages: Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini.

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model.

Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context.

Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead.
Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

extraction.body: Your Google data can act as an extra reference point for Nano Banana 2. Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini. After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

sources.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
passages: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.
Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language.
Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.
Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto.
That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence.
This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

extraction.body: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products. The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle. The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed. Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said. That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said. extraction.body: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” [Video: Personal Intelligence in cars] Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle. The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed. Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. At the start of the year, Google debuted Personal Intelligence , a Gemini feature that allows the chatbot to pull information from your other Google apps to generate more personalized responses. An expansion in March brought Personal Intelligence to free accounts after it was previously only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. And now Google has begun rolling out the feature to Android Auto users. In practice, the company says today's update will improve Gemini's reasoning capabilities in cars. It will also make the assistant capable of delivering more specific details as they relate to your questions and prompts. For example, if you're driving to the airport, Google suggests Gemini with Personal Intelligence will be able to answer questions like "what's my flight gate?" and "is my flight on time?" Provided you've linked your Gmail account, it can do all this without you needing to pull over to find a confirmation email. More broadly, Google says Personal Intelligence makes it easier to interact with Gemini more naturally. For instance, if you need directions to your doctor's office, you can just say "take me to my doctor's appointment," instead of speaking a specific address. Recommendations are also improved. If you're in a new city, Google suggests you can ask for dinner spots along your driving route and Gemini will generate suggestions while factoring in preferences and restrictions, like if you're a vegetarian. sources.title: Oracle posts 30% revenue growth fueled by AI cloud demand as debts hits $125 billion - CNBC
passages: Oracle shares whipsawed on Friday after the software company reported 30% revenue growth for the latest quarter, topping estimates, with sales fueled by strong demand for cloud infrastructure.
Alongside selling its flagship database software, Oracle now has $125 billion in debt as it funds an expansive buildout of data centers for AI workloads.
The investment is expected to expand capacity for contracted cloud demand from customers including Nvidia, Meta, OpenAI, Advanced Micro Devices and SpaceX's AI business.
The company guided to second-quarter revenue growth of 30% to 34%, with cloud revenue rising between 64% and 70%.
It expects total revenue for the 2027 fiscal year to be at least $90 billion.
Oracle delivered an additional 850 megawatts of data center capacity in the quarter.
It also booked over $30 billion in further AI cloud contracts, and delivered more than 300,000 graphics processing units to its AI Cloud customers.
Oracle posted $5.4 billion in negative free cash flow during the quarter, versus a negative $362 million a year earlier.
Oracle's outlook for 2027 is "modest," and the company's management framework is "conservative," the analysts said.
WATCH: Oracle shares spike on earnings and revenue
Fiscal first-quarter revenue increased to $19.35 billion, beating LSEG consensus estimates of $19.14 billion.
Even with Friday's rally, Oracle is down about 20% this year on concern about the hefty amount of debt the company has raised to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
Citi analysts reiterated their buy rating in a Friday note, saying Oracle had met expectations and "cleared the runway" for its upcoming investor day.

passages: SpaceX announced revenues of $14.6 billion in its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, which it says was a growth of 161 percent year-over-year “fueled by our Super Intelligence (SI) segment and accelerated growth in Connectivity.” While its Space division posted a $7 million loss in income from operations, its Connectivity group posted income from operations $2.4 billion and its SI group posted $431 million.

SpaceX is livestreamed a video of its earnings call on X, where Elon Musk said that SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster next month, that Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, and that its Starlink connectivity business could generate “several hundred billion dollars a year.” This is the second earnings report from SpaceX after the company’s IPO in June.

The company’s so-called “SI” business saw revenues of $7.6 billion, which were up 830 percent year-over-year, “primarily driven” by “the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor, and increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers.” For its Connectivity business, SpaceX reported revenues of $5.2 billion and 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers. Space business revenues were $1.8 billion, up six percent year-over-year. SpaceX is livestreamed a video of its earnings call on X, where Elon Musk said that SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster next month, that Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, and that its Starlink connectivity business could generate “several hundred billion dollars a year.” This is the second earnings report from SpaceX after the company’s IPO in June. The earnings follow a busy Q3 for Elon Musk’s rocket, AI, and social media company, which included the official closing of its $60 billion deal to acquire AI coding tool Cursor, the 13th launch of SpaceX’s Starship, and the launch of a new V5 Starlink residential dish. During the Q2 earnings call, president Gwynne Shotwell described plans to build out a terrestrial mobile network to compete with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon. In SpaceX’s Q2 earnings, the company also noted that its “connectivity” business, which encompasses Starlink, didn’t have a loss from operations, while its AI and space businesses did. Tesla, where Musk is also CEO, reports earnings on Wednesday. Update, October 20th: Added details from the Q3 earnings call.

sources.title: [Space Exploration Technologies Q3 2026 Earnings Call] SpaceX Revenue Soars 161% to $14.6B as AI Compute Ignites Explosive Growth; Q1 2027 Revenue Guidance Set at $33-37B - BigGo Finance
passages: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity.
Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion.
SpaceX’s Q3 results reflect a company firing on all cylinders, with the SI segment emerging as its largest and fastest-growing business.
The aggressive capital expenditure plans and ambitious revenue targets underscore management’s conviction in the AI compute opportunity.
However, the capital-intensive nature of the build-out, potential execution challenges in chip fabrication and power infrastructure, and the high hurdle for a Tesla merger remain key risks.
For now, investors are likely to focus on the massive revenue guidance for Q1 2027 and the company’s ability to scale compute capacity at an unprecedented pace.
The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute.
For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts.
He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling.
“If you just look at the rate at which we are actually deploying and turning on compute, I’m being as precise as possible about this,” he said.

“It is absolutely insane to be deploying, providing the power and all the electrical equipment, the cooling, the batteries, the networking, and everything else that’s needed to turn on 220,000 GB300s a month.” Garlinghouse added that the company has an investment-grade balance sheet and multiple debt capital pools available.
“These are very aggressive dates,” he acknowledged, thanking ASML and other suppliers for accelerating equipment deliveries.
Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year.
On V3 satellite capacity: Shotwell said a few hundred V3 satellites are needed for users to really feel the impact, and she expects to achieve that by mid-2027.

Oracle shares whipsawed on Friday after the software company reported 30% revenue growth for the latest quarter, topping estimates, with sales fueled by strong demand for cloud infrastructure.

It also booked over $30 billion in further AI cloud contracts, and delivered more than 300,000 graphics processing units to its AI Cloud customers.
Oracle posted $5.4 billion in negative free cash flow during the quarter, versus a negative $362 million a year earlier.
Oracle's outlook for 2027 is "modest," and the company's management framework is "conservative," the analysts said.

Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity.
Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion.
SpaceX’s Q3 results reflect a company firing on all cylinders, with the SI segment emerging as its largest and fastest-growing business.
The aggressive capital expenditure plans and ambitious revenue targets underscore management’s conviction in the AI compute opportunity.
However, the capital-intensive nature of the build-out, potential execution challenges in chip fabrication and power infrastructure, and the high hurdle for a Tesla merger remain key risks.
For now, investors are likely to focus on the massive revenue guidance for Q1 2027 and the company’s ability to scale compute capacity at an unprecedented pace.
The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute.
For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts.
He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling.
“If you just look at the rate at which we are actually deploying and turning on compute, I’m being as precise as possible about this,” he said.

“It is absolutely insane to be deploying, providing the power and all the electrical equipment, the cooling, the batteries, the networking, and everything else that’s needed to turn on 220,000 GB300s a month.” Garlinghouse added that the company has an investment-grade balance sheet and multiple debt capital pools available.
“These are very aggressive dates,” he acknowledged, thanking ASML and other suppliers for accelerating equipment deliveries.
Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year.
On V3 satellite capacity: Shotwell said a few hundred V3 satellites are needed for users to really feel the impact, and she expects to achieve that by mid-2027.

passages: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity.
Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion.
SpaceX’s Q3 results reflect a company firing on all cylinders, with the SI segment emerging as its largest and fastest-growing business.
The aggressive capital expenditure plans and ambitious revenue targets underscore management’s conviction in the AI compute opportunity.
However, the capital-intensive nature of the build-out, potential execution challenges in chip fabrication and power infrastructure, and the high hurdle for a Tesla merger remain key risks.
For now, investors are likely to focus on the massive revenue guidance for Q1 2027 and the company’s ability to scale compute capacity at an unprecedented pace.
The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute.
For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts.
He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling.
“If you just look at the rate at which we are actually deploying and turning on compute, I’m being as precise as possible about this,” he said.

“It is absolutely insane to be deploying, providing the power and all the electrical equipment, the cooling, the batteries, the networking, and everything else that’s needed to turn on 220,000 GB300s a month.” Garlinghouse added that the company has an investment-grade balance sheet and multiple debt capital pools available.
“These are very aggressive dates,” he acknowledged, thanking ASML and other suppliers for accelerating equipment deliveries.

extraction.body: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity. Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity, and super intelligence,” CEO Elon Musk declared at the start of the earnings call, held live from the company’s Starlink factory in Bastrop, Texas. The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute. The SI segment alone generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up $5 billion quarter-over-quarter and $6.7 billion year-over-year, fueled by the ramp of cloud services agreements and the mid-quarter acquisition of Cursor. Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year. Space segment revenue reached $1.8 billion, up 84% sequentially but only 6% year-over-year, reflecting a favorable customer mix. SpaceX launched 35 rockets in Q3, including 21 Starlink Falcon 9 missions, two Starship flights, one Falcon Heavy, and 12 customer missions. The company secured 18 new national security space launch missions and three additional human spaceflight missions on Dragon. Connectivity revenue rose 69% year-over-year and 22% sequentially to $5.2 billion. Starlink consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million, adding 1.6 million in the quarter. Monthly ARPU increased 5% sequentially to $69. Enterprise and government revenue jumped 91% year-over-year, highlighted by Starshield and aviation contracts now covering roughly 12,000 planes—nearly a quarter of the available aircraft worldwide. “Starlink is now contracted for roughly 12,000 planes, almost a quarter of the available aircraft,” said CFO Gwynne Shotwell, adding that Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa Airlines, Korean Air, Austrian Airlines, and Asiana Airlines all flew their first Starlink-equipped aircraft during the quarter. Starlink Mobile surpassed 22 million monthly users, up 37% quarter-over-quarter. The company also received FCC approval to launch 15,000 mobile V2 satellites and announced an agreement to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum. SI segment revenue of $7.6 billion included $608 million from Cursor, which closed mid-quarter. Excluding Cursor, SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially, driven primarily by the activation of new cloud services agreements. SI segment adjusted EBITDA was $5 billion, up $3.8 billion quarter-over-quarter. Operating income was $431 million; excluding $1.2 billion in stock-based compensation from Cursor, operating profit was $1.6 billion. “We ended the third quarter with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity, with additional data halls already online in early October,” said Brad Garlinghouse, CFO. “We expect to have nearly 2 gigawatts by the end of October and 2.5-3 gigawatts by the end of the fourth quarter.” The company noted that new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year at current pricing, which is tracking slightly above the high end of the $30-$50 per watt range discussed last quarter. SpaceX launched Starship Flight 14 in the final week of the quarter, which reached orbit and deployed operational Starlink V3 satellites—a key milestone. Flight 15, scheduled for November, will attempt to catch both the booster and the ship. “If we succeed, it will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered,” Musk said. “This is a massive technology milestone. The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle.” Musk also announced the Louisiana Spaceport, targeting first launch in 2028 with high confidence in 2029. The company expects Starship to fly weekly in the first half of 2027 and twice weekly or more by the end of 2027. For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts. He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling. On Terafab and chip fabrication: Musk said internal expectations are for a first test chip to be functional around May or June 2027 at the Austin research fab, with volume production targeted for Q3 2028 at Terafab in Gibbons Creek. “These are very aggressive dates,” he acknowledged, thanking ASML and other suppliers for accelerating equipment deliveries. On power constraints and funding: Musk revealed that SpaceX is currently turning on 220,000 GB300s per month and has a proprietary plan to reach 20 gigawatts of incremental power and cooling by end-2027. “If you just look at the rate at which we are actually deploying and turning on compute, I’m being as precise as possible about this,” he said. “It is absolutely insane to be deploying, providing the power and all the electrical equipment, the cooling, the batteries, the networking, and everything else that’s needed to turn on 220,000 GB300s a month.” Garlinghouse added that the company has an investment-grade balance sheet and multiple debt capital pools available. On a potential Tesla merger: Musk addressed the long-rumored combination, stating that both companies have formed special committees of independent directors. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. “Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes. At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” He noted that any deal would require a 50% vote of all Tesla shares, a high hurdle. No agreement on terms has been reached. On Starlink Mobile: Shotwell noted that 85-93% of mobile connectivity is via Wi-Fi and that Starlink broadband supports that. She expects S-band spectrum to carry the majority of traffic, with low-band spectrum providing critical building penetration. Musk added that the company sees a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue and will detail the plan in a future presentation. On compute allocation: Musk said the goal is roughly a 50/50 split between internal and external compute use, with flexibility to shift 60/40 either way. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone,” he said. “That is why I posted that video meme of the Monty Python Cheese Shop sketch, where the guy goes into a cheese shop to get some cheese, and they actually have no cheese.” He added that short-term contracts are renewing at higher dollars per watt, and that a six-month payback period for compute next year is not impossible. On V3 satellite capacity: Shotwell said a few hundred V3 satellites are needed for users to really feel the impact, and she expects to achieve that by mid-2027. On Louisiana Spaceport: Musk said the internal aspiration for first launch from Louisiana is 2028, with 2029 highly likely for at-scale launches. “I’m highly confident,” he said. SpaceX’s Q3 results reflect a company firing on all cylinders, with the SI segment emerging as its largest and fastest-growing business. The aggressive capital expenditure plans and ambitious revenue targets underscore management’s conviction in the AI compute opportunity. However, the capital-intensive nature of the build-out, potential execution challenges in chip fabrication and power infrastructure, and the high hurdle for a Tesla merger remain key risks. For now, investors are likely to focus on the massive revenue guidance for Q1 2027 and the company’s ability to scale compute capacity at an unprecedented pace. passages: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday.

Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call.
OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind.

sources.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
passages: OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI said its goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work required to turn those discoveries into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine takes roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery through regulatory approval in the United States, according to the company, and the teams behind those programs must coordinate work across internal departments and external partners, often through disconnected systems. OpenAI describes the present moment as an inflection point at which AI can take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind is OpenAI’s life sciences brand. OpenAI said that together the organizations aim to build agents that connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio built its platform around a model in which people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, which OpenAI says frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. According to OpenAI, a problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others: a failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents pinpoint the activities and timelines a problem touches, pull together the relevant information, and compare response options, and scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Orchestra Bio confirmed the acquisition on its own website, saying it started the company four years earlier to help biotech and pharma teams advance their drug development programs. The company describes medicine development as involving thousands of decisions and dependencies that run across discovery, preclinical, manufacturing, and clinical work. In its framing, agents can take on planning, orchestration, and analysis, leaving scientists and program leaders to concentrate on the decisions that require their expertise. Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters. Rosalind Workbench is in research preview, with an orchestrated set of scientific tools connected in a single workspace. It offers an Explore mode for general scientific questions, using the latest ChatGPT models available to the user, and a Research mode that applies GPT-Rosalind to more complex biological questions, in-depth analysis, and advanced research workflows, with access through an application process. Researchers can also use GPT-Rosalind inside Codex to connect their scientific tools, data, and evidence into research workflows that teams can review, share, and reuse, while a GPT-Rosalind API targets organizations that want to integrate life sciences reasoning into their own research applications, internal tools, and governed workflows. API access is subject to eligibility review and organizational approval. OpenAI’s product page reports benchmark results for the model on life sciences research tasks, stated as increases in performance per token: 53.7% on Genebench, 18.0% on Medchem Bench, 19.6% on Labworkbench, and 4.42% on LifeSci Bench. The page lists supported uses that include prioritizing biological targets, engineering proteins, synthesizing evidence across papers and experiments, analyzing unstructured experimental results, and saving workflows that teams can inspect, share, and reuse. OpenAI said its partnership with Novo Nordisk is aimed at translating the drugmaker’s scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance, and that at Moderna, AI is helping teams turn insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. The Rosalind Academic Plan offers eligible labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery. An enterprise option brings GPT-Rosalind into approved research workflows with governance review and enterprise-grade deployment controls, while government and public-health teams can request reviewed access for research, preparedness, and resilience work under what OpenAI describes as clear public-benefit boundaries. A separate Rosalind Biodefense program supports trusted developers and public-health teams building defensive applications with GPT-Rosalind, with focus areas that include early detection, preparedness, diagnostics, response, and medical countermeasures. OpenAI said its broader vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines, and it described bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind as a step toward that vision. coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday.

Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call.
OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind.
Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other.
OpenAI says the combined team will build agents that connect scientific findings with the decisions and follow-up studies needed to turn a promising result into an actual medicine.
Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists.
In April, OpenAI launched GPT-Rosalind , a model built specifically for biology and drug discovery, and restricted it to vetted U.S. enterprise customers such as Amgen and Moderna.
In January alone, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health , which lets users connect their medical records to the chatbot, and bought records startup Torch for a reported $100 million to build it out.

Anthropic, OpenAI's closest rival, has been running the same play: it bought AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April and launched a research platform called Claude Science in June.
OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a company whose platform coordinates drug development work across biopharma teams, and is bringing the startup’s team and technology together with Rosalind, its AI models and tools for life sciences research.

Orchestra adds a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development.

An enterprise option brings GPT-Rosalind into approved research workflows with governance review and enterprise-grade deployment controls, while government and public-health teams can request reviewed access for research, preparedness, and resilience work under what OpenAI describes as clear public-benefit boundaries.
Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters.

"Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner," OpenAI said in the announcement. Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists. The financial terms were not disclosed. Getting a new medicine from first idea to U.S. approval takes time—up to 15 years according to OpenAI. Every month shaved off that timeline is a month earlier that a new treatment can reach the people waiting for it, and a month earlier that the company can generate cash. The process is also absurdly expensive: bringing one approved drug to market can cost more than $2.6 billion, and fewer than 10% of candidates that enter human testing ever make it to pharmacy shelves. Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other. Those partners usually include contract research organizations, the outside labs hired to run studies, and contract manufacturers that produce the experimental drug. Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call. Founded in the fall of 2022, Orchestra raised its seed round from Andreessen Horowitz, Definition Capital, Insight Partners, and 8VC, and about $20 million in total, according to Caplight data. The company should not be confused with Orchestra BioMed, an unrelated Nasdaq-listed medical device maker that trades under the ticker OBIO. OpenAI announced the acquisition on October 20, 2026. OpenAI said its goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work required to turn those discoveries into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine takes roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery through regulatory approval in the United States, according to the company, and the teams behind those programs must coordinate work across internal departments and external partners, often through disconnected systems. OpenAI describes the present moment as an inflection point at which AI can take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind is OpenAI’s life sciences brand. OpenAI describes GPT-Rosalind as a purpose-built model that helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry, and Rosalind Workbench as the layer that connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data so researchers can analyze results and plan experiments. Orchestra adds a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. OpenAI said that together the organizations aim to build agents that connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio built its platform around a model in which people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, which OpenAI says frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. According to OpenAI, a problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others: a failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents pinpoint the activities and timelines a problem touches, pull together the relevant information, and compare response options, and scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Orchestra Bio confirmed the acquisition on its own website, saying it started the company four years earlier to help biotech and pharma teams advance their drug development programs. The company describes medicine development as involving thousands of decisions and dependencies that run across discovery, preclinical, manufacturing, and clinical work. In its framing, agents can take on planning, orchestration, and analysis, leaving scientists and program leaders to concentrate on the decisions that require their expertise. Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters. Rosalind Workbench is in research preview, with an orchestrated set of scientific tools connected in a single workspace. It offers an Explore mode for general scientific questions, using the latest ChatGPT models available to the user, and a Research mode that applies GPT-Rosalind to more complex biological questions, in-depth analysis, and advanced research workflows, with access through an application process. Researchers can also use GPT-Rosalind inside Codex to connect their scientific tools, data, and evidence into research workflows that teams can review, share, and reuse, while a GPT-Rosalind API targets organizations that want to integrate life sciences reasoning into their own research applications, internal tools, and governed workflows. API access is subject to eligibility review and organizational approval. OpenAI’s product page reports benchmark results for the model on life sciences research tasks, stated as increases in performance per token: 53.7% on Genebench, 18.0% on Medchem Bench, 19.6% on Labworkbench, and 4.42% on LifeSci Bench. The page lists supported uses that include prioritizing biological targets, engineering proteins, synthesizing evidence across papers and experiments, analyzing unstructured experimental results, and saving workflows that teams can inspect, share, and reuse. OpenAI said its partnership with Novo Nordisk is aimed at translating the drugmaker’s scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance, and that at Moderna, AI is helping teams turn insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. In a statement carried on OpenAI’s Rosalind page , Mike Doustdar, Novo Nordisk’s CEO and president, said: “Our partnership with OpenAI will help translate this scale into faster R&D and commercial execution, while maintaining the governance our patients and society expect.” OpenAI also lists structured access routes beyond enterprise customers. The Rosalind Academic Plan offers eligible labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery. An enterprise option brings GPT-Rosalind into approved research workflows with governance review and enterprise-grade deployment controls, while government and public-health teams can request reviewed access for research, preparedness, and resilience work under what OpenAI describes as clear public-benefit boundaries. A separate Rosalind Biodefense program supports trusted developers and public-health teams building defensive applications with GPT-Rosalind, with focus areas that include early detection, preparedness, diagnostics, response, and medical countermeasures. OpenAI said its broader vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines, and it described bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind as a step toward that vision. He said a merger would require support from both sets of shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. Musk spoke about the potential tie-up during a call with Wall Street analysts about SpaceX’s quarterly results, which surpassed estimates; the company’s revenue more than doubled in part from renting out computing capacity to other artificial intelligence firms. In January, Tesla announced that it was investing about $2 billion to acquire shares in an AI startup that’s a subsidiary of SpaceX. Musk said that, because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations, he is not a member of either special committee or involved in the talks. He said the committees consist of the two boards’ independent directors but did not specify the memberships. “It’s an odd Kabuki dance, where groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” he said during the earnings calls. He also said that even answering a question about the idea from an analyst felt like “dancing through a minefield.” Musk, though, endorsed the idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies, as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” he said. Musk has already consolidated some of his other holdings. Last year, he merged his social media company, X, with his AI startup, called at the time xAI. Then, in February, SpaceX acquired xAI , which Musk has since renamed SpaceXSI.

He cautioned against assuming a deal is inevitable. "I do not think we should necessarily assume that… a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. I think that would be overstating it." Musk added that he personally views a combination as a good idea, but emphasized that any transaction would require broad shareholder support. On the Tesla side, he noted, approval would need a majority of all outstanding shares—not merely a majority of shares voted—creating what he called "quite a high hurdle." "At this point, the special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction," Musk said. "Obviously, there's no guarantee that they will." While SPCX shares traded 8% higher after hours at the time of writing, TSLA was up 2%. Musk, however, outlined what he sees as the strategic rationale, pointing to overlapping work in "superintelligence," or the company's term for artificial intelligence endeavors. Last week, Barclays said that they expect a merger announcement could arrive either tied to the shareholder meeting or in the coming 6-12 months, so it could be closed during the Trump Administration. sources.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
passages: The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger.
The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing .
It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.
Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent.
Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX.
Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.
Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane

extraction.body: The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing . Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance. SpaceX lists six independent directors , including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelef Boutha are also considered independent directors. Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements. Musk said he supports the idea of the merger, but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said. The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX. sources.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
passages: The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger.
The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing .
It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.
Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent.
Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX.
Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.
Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane

extraction.body: The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing . Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance. SpaceX lists six independent directors , including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelef Boutha are also considered independent directors. Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements. Musk said he supports the idea of the merger, but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said. The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX. extraction.body: Tech billionaire Elon Musk said Tuesday that the boards of SpaceX and Tesla had separately formed special committees to discuss the idea of a merger, taking a small step toward the possible consolidation of his two biggest companies. Musk, who is the CEO of both companies, said that the special committees had not reached an agreement and that there was no guarantee they would. He said a merger would require support from both sets of shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. Musk spoke about the potential tie-up during a call with Wall Street analysts about SpaceX’s quarterly results, which surpassed estimates; the company’s revenue more than doubled in part from renting out computing capacity to other artificial intelligence firms. In January, Tesla announced that it was investing about $2 billion to acquire shares in an AI startup that’s a subsidiary of SpaceX. Musk said that, because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations, he is not a member of either special committee or involved in the talks. He said the committees consist of the two boards’ independent directors but did not specify the memberships. “It’s an odd Kabuki dance, where groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” he said during the earnings calls. He also said that even answering a question about the idea from an analyst felt like “dancing through a minefield.” Musk, though, endorsed the idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies, as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” he said. Musk has already consolidated some of his other holdings. Last year, he merged his social media company, X, with his AI startup, called at the time xAI. Then, in February, SpaceX acquired xAI, which Musk has since renamed SpaceXSI.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. Flight 14 is also slated to put Starlink V3 satellites into an operational orbit for the first time. Two steps sit between here and the attempt: the preflight engine firings both vehicles still have to complete, and the regulatory sign-off Musk named. The company's towers have caught the returning Super Heavy booster before, but never the Ship, which comes back from space at far higher speeds. The reason a catch matters is money. Starship's economics rest on both halves of the rocket flying again quickly -- a booster and Ship recovered at the tower are meant to be turned around and reflown instead of rebuilt. And a tower catch is the version of reuse that saves the most. The vehicle lands where it launched, gets inspected, and gets restacked, with no ocean recovery in between. For now, the finances run through Starlink. The V3 satellites Flight 14 would carry are the larger generation that the network's next capacity step depends on. Of course, a tentative date is just that. The flight could slip into September, and the regulatory review isn't on the company's clock. A missed catch wouldn't end the program, either. Test flights exist to find the failures. But a catch that works would be the first time the Ship itself came back to the tower. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . SpaceX will soon notch a huge spaceflight milestone, if all goes according to plan. The company will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's quarter 3 (Q3) earnings call today (Oct. 20). If SpaceX succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," Musk said. "The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle. So this is, I think, a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness." Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked. As Musk noted, both of its stages — the Super Heavy booster and Ship spacecraft — are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX thinks will make Mars settlement and other grand exploration feats economically feasible. Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages). Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters come back to Earth on landing pads near the launch site or on ships at sea downrange. Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms. This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030. Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does. Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.) "I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year." Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever . It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft . The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30. And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion. Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence"). SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year. "In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said. SpaceX will soon notch a huge spaceflight milestone, if all goes according to plan.

The company will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's quarter 3 (Q3) earnings call today (Oct. 20).

If SpaceX succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," Musk said. "The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle. So this is, I think, a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness."
Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked.

As Musk noted, both of its stages — the Super Heavy booster and Ship spacecraft — are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX thinks will make Mars settlement and other grand exploration feats economically feasible.

Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages). Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters come back to Earth on landing pads near the launch site or on ships at sea downrange. Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms.

This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030.

Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does.
Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.)

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year."

Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever . It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft .

The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30.

And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion.

Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence").

SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year.
"In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said.

He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

extraction.body: SpaceX is planning to launch its next Starship test flight as soon as this month, CEO Elon Musk said on August 4 at the company's first earnings call. The mission will send the first upgraded Starlink satellites into orbit. It will also try to land the rocket's massive upper stage for the first time. This marks a big step up from the last test in July, when the upper stage showed better landing skills over the Indian Ocean. However, the plan still depends on getting regulatory approval, Musk said, adding that Starship's launch pace should "increase rapidly" in the coming months.Landing the upper stage, known as the "ship," is key to SpaceX's goal of building the world's first fully reusable orbital rocket system. Musk wants to use this system to grow the Starlink broadband network. NASA is also watching closely, since it plans to use Starship as a moon lander.SpaceX to seek regulatory approval for its next rocket launch dateSpaceX is currently pulling the 13th test's rocket stage out of the ocean for inspection, based on satellite images from Vantor. During the earnings call, Elon Musk said the exact launch date, and whether the ship will attempt a landing, depends on approval from regulators. "Assuming we receive regulatory approval to do so, we'll attempt to catch the ship with the tower on the next flight, which is tentatively scheduled for the end of this month," Musk said.The 14th Starship flight will carry the first batch of V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. Elon Musk said these satellites are "expected to deliver 10 times the amount of broadband capacity and data density from our current generations." SpaceX has said in its IPO prospectus that it eventually wants to launch 60 such satellites per Starship mission, across dozens of future flights.How the catch-and-land system worksA successful landing would mean catching the ship using giant mechanical arms on the launch tower in Texas. SpaceX has already used these arms to catch the rocket's Super Heavy booster three times, most recently in March 2025. Musk's long-term goal is for the tower to catch both parts. Super Heavy would be caught first, then quickly moved aside. About 90 minutes later, the ship would return after circling Earth and get caught too."Probably a year from now, we will be doing at least one flight a day, possibly more," Musk said at the earnings call.Get the latest technology news and updates.
