Prior to joining the Center for Data Innovation, Eline Chivot worked for several years in the Netherlands as policy analyst in a leading think tank, where her work included research projects on defense, security and economic policy issues. More recently, Eline worked at one of Brussels’ largest trade associations and managed its relations with representatives of the digital tech industry in Europe and beyond. In the first model, firms mostly adopt general-purpose, standardized AI services. [127] Similar to China, the United States has large technology firms, including Google and Amazon, that are providing these services. In the second model of adoption, AI start-ups focused on creating products and services to solve specific problems, such as drone delivery, disrupt traditional businesses using AI. [128] The United States is well positioned in this AI-uptake scenario as well because of its breadth and depth of well-funded AI start-ups.

While the United States may be in the lead in AI development, it is not clear it will maintain its lead. Multiple analyses of funding data for AI start-ups, including this one, have found at least one year where Chinese AI start-ups received more funding than U.S. start-ups. For example, Chinese AI start-ups received an estimated $8.1 billion in investment in 2017, compared with an estimated $6.2 billion for U.S. start-ups. [129] In addition, research by Tencent, a Chinese technology company, found the average time for an AI start-up to receive investment was 14.8 months in the United States, compared with 9.7 months in China. [130]

China has also begun to close its large gap to the United States in terms of the number of investments in AI start-ups, reducing the difference from 476 investments in 2016 to 371 in 2018. [131] The smaller gap is both due to significant growth in the number of investments in Chinese start-ups and relatively stagnant growth in the number of deals involving U.S. AI start-ups. U.S. AI start-ups did receive a record amount of investment in 2018, however, receiving an estimated $10.7 billion in investment, while Chinese AI start-ups received an estimated $5.4 billion in funding. [132] Data on financing in 2019 should help clarify whether the United States will be able to maintain its lead, or China will be able to match, or surpass, the United States in funding consistently.

While private equity and venture capital funding for EU AI start-ups nearly tripled between 2016 and 2018, the European Union is firmly behind the United States and China. [133] For example, the United States received more funding in any year between 2016 and 2018 than the European Union received in the three years combined. [134] Similarly, Chinese AI start-ups received billions of more dollars in private equity and venture capital funding than the EU in both 2017 and 2018. Unless EU start-ups begin to garner significantly more funding, the European Union is at risk of falling further behind the United States and China.

It is difficult for the European Union to compete against the United States and China in AI funding in part because its investments, while noteworthy in number, are typically smaller. For example, a vast majority (70 percent) of EU’s 2018 private equity and venture capital funding AI was through seed or angel rounds (rounds in which investors help new and small companies gain traction). [135] Indeed, roughly 45 percent of investments made in U.S. or Chinese AI start-ups in 2018 were part of seed or angel rounds. Due to the high risk of firms seeking such seed or angel funding not succeeding, the rounds typically involve transactions that total between $10,000 and $2 million. In contrast, Series C funding rounds, which are for more-established companies, are usually at least $10 million, and are often much larger. For example, the average Series C deal for a U.S. AI company in 2018 was nearly $61 million. [136] The EU lacks such transactions, however—only 1 percent of deals going to EU AI start-ups in 2018 were part of a Series C round, compared with 5 percent and 6 percent in the United States and China. [137] In addition, EU funding deals are almost always smaller on average, no matter the funding stage. For example, between 2016 and 2018, the average size of Chinese deals was larger than EU deals at the seed/angel, Series A, Series B, and Series C stages. [138] Similarly, the median U.S. deal has been larger than the median EU deal the past three years. These figures match anecdotal accounts that characterize Europe’s start-up market as traditionally fraught with barriers, even though it is improving. For example, Irina Haivas, a principal at Atomico , a global technology investment firm, noted that in Europe there are barriers “to tech transfer and IP, access to funding to scale capital-intensive, research-based businesses, and to some degree, a perception barrier around the feasibility of ‘commercially-driven,’ non-academic careers.” [139]

Technological innovation is key to raising standards of living, and AI is likely to be a primary driver of technological innovation in the emerging innovation wave. [140] Indeed, AI adoption is estimated to create $13 trillion of gross domestic product (GDP) growth by 2030. [141] Firms increasingly need to adopt AI in order to remain competitive in the global economy because it allows them to automate and optimize many facets of their business, derive faster and more accurate insights from data, and develop new products and services. As a result, countries where businesses are late adopters will lag in the global economy. [142] In addition to the economic gains, AI stands to enable important societal gains, such as reducing automobile accidents and injuries and enabling better treatment of diseases. [143]

The governments of China, the European Union, and the United States have each publicly recognized the importance of AI adoption. For example, China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released the “Three-Year Action Plan for Promoting the Development of a New Generation of Artificial Intelligence Industry (2018–2020)” in 2017, which called for the integration of AI in the manufacturing industry. [144] In addition, the EU’s coordinated plan on AI calls for the creation of “common European data spaces” in sectors such as manufacturing and energy to support the development and adoption of AI. [145] Lastly, U.S. President Trump issued an executive order in 2019 that called for the creation of technical standards to enable the adoption of AI. [146]

To assess the level of AI adoption in China, the European Union, and the United States, we analyzed surveys regarding AI adoption. We allotted this section 10 of 100 available points. On an absolute basis, China led (7.7 points) over the European Union (1.3) and United States (1). In terms of the percentage of firms adopting or piloting AI, China led (4.7 points), followed by the United States (2.9 points) and the European Union (2.5 points).

Mobile Payments (2018): Consumers also generate data technology firms can analyze each time they use a mobile device to purchase a product. We define ”mobile payments” as using a mobile device to scan, tap, swipe, or check in order to make a point-of-sale transaction, which does not include purchases such as those of digital goods on mobile devices. [174] Over 525 million Chinese individuals were estimated to have made a mobile payment in 2018, compared with 55 million in the United States and an estimated 44 million people in the European Union. [175] An estimated 45 percent of the Chinese population used mobile payments in 2018, compared with 20 percent for the United States, 13 percent for the United Kingdom, and 8 percent for Germany. [176]

China leads in both data collected and likely the amount of data available to large Internet firms, which are also the firms best leveraging AI. This fact, combined with multiple data deficiencies that changes in Chinese policies could alleviate, means China could have an even bigger advantage in the future.

Large Chinese Internet firms likely have a data advantage compared with their Western counterparts for at least two reasons. First, services in the West are relatively divided between firms. For example, Amazon users are able to buy groceries but not book a hotel. Chinese technology companies, on the other hand, have created all-in-one super apps. For example, Kai-Fu Lee has written that WeChat, an app owned by Chinese technology company Tencent, allows users to “hail a taxi, order a meal, book a hotel, manage a phone bill, and buy a flight to the United States, all without ever leaving the app.” [215] In the United States, these services, and thus the data, are divided between such firms as Uber, Postmates, Expedia, Verizon, and Venmo. [216]

Second, Chinese technology companies have embedded themselves in traditionally off-line activities. For example, Didi, the Chinese equivalent of Uber, has bought gas stations and auto repair shops. In addition, Meituan Dianping, whose origins are similar to that of Yelp, not only provides users with a platform to compare businesses, but also handles food delivery. [217] Chinese Internet companies are therefore afforded the opportunity to collect a greater variety and depth of data than their American counterparts. [218] It should be noted, however, that the broader global reach of some U.S. technology giants provides them with their own data advantage. For example, Facebook has more than 2 billion users, while WeChat has only 1.1 billion users. Should Chinese firms achieve more success internationally, such as with the social media video app TikTok, the U.S. advantage will diminish. [219]

AI systems rely on semiconductor devices, such as integrated circuits, that can perform large numbers of operations per second. Indeed, graphics processing units (GPUs), which are circuits that perform mathematical operations in parallel, have catalyzed recent AI developments. [226] In addition, technologies such as supercomputers, which combine processing units such as GPUs and central processing units, can expand the capabilities of AI systems through massive computational power. For example, researchers have combined supercomputers and machine learning techniques to model climate change as well as the merging of blackholes. [227]

The aforementioned hardware is important to a nation’s AI competitiveness for several reasons. First, nations with a weak semiconductor industry can be vulnerable to the actions of other countries. For example, in 2018, the United States banned American companies from providing parts and software to ZTE, a large Chinese telecommunications equipment manufacturer. Due to ZTE’s reliance on semiconductor devices from U.S. firms, the company nearly folded. While the United States ultimately lifted the ban, the situation highlighted China’s dependence on Western technology. [228] More recently, the United States has blocked U.S. firms from selling chips to five specific supercomputing entities, and the U.S. Commerce Department has black listed Huawei, which prevents firms from selling U.S. technology to Huawei without a license. [229] Second, many experts believe AI chips designed specifically for AI applications, such as autonomous vehicles or facial recognition, will outperform such proven technologies as GPUs. [230] As a result, non-semiconductor firms, such as Apple, Alphabet, and Amazon, are designing their own AI chips to meet their specific needs, which could increase the performance of their AI systems and thereby provide them with a competitive advantage. [231] Third, high-performance computing has fueled breakthrough discoveries in several sectors, and access to the best performing supercomputers provides nations an advantage in developing leading-edge weapons systems and applications faster than other nations. [232]

This section analyzes China, the European Union, and the United States in terms of semiconductor sales, semiconductor R&D spending, the number of firms designing AI chips, the number of supercomputers ranked in the top 500 by performance, and the aggregate system performance of the supercomputers. We allotted this category 10 of the 100 available points. On an absolute basis, the most recent data available showed the United States leading in hardware (6 points), followed by China (2.5) and the European Union (1.5). Controlling for workforce sizes, the United States (7.6 points) led the European Union (1.5) and China (0.8).

China’s large population gives it a significant data advantage over other nations. However, China limits the size of this advantage through a weak open data culture and a lack of standardized data formats.

Several Chinese AI chip start-ups have recently received hundreds of millions of dollars in funding and firms such as Huawei have developed impressive chip designs. [276] Nonetheless, the complexity of developing chips, China’s shortage of talent, and the lack of multiple Chinese semiconductor firms being in the top 15 globally for sales indicate China still needs to make significant progress in order to match the United States in semiconductors. China should also stop unfair trade practices such as forced technology transfers and intellectual property theft, which have led to increased scrutiny of its firms by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) and put its ability to use Western semiconductors and designs in peril. Computing power used to be a commodity China could easily procure. [277]

The European Union has the talent to compete with China and the United States in AI. However, EU researchers frequently leave for U.S. firms, and the EU has a smaller AI venture capital ecosystem compared with China and the United States.

The EU should not subject new digitally-based business models to the same regulation as incumbents—which often limits innovation. Instead, the EU should focus on providing equal protection, not equal regulation. As part of an EU strategy:

The United States is still the global leader in AI. The Obama administration initiated some steps to support AI through the National Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Strategic Plan, which the Trump administration has since expanded on. For example, President Trump launched the American AI Initiative in 2019 through an executive order. [297] The order seeks to improve AI R&D, workforce development, and international engagement. [298]

While the executive order is important in ensuring U.S. leadership, the government can do more. In particular, Congress should reform immigration rules and increase research funding. It is also critical for Congress to avoid overly restrictive policies, including data protection rules, that would discourage the use of AI.

[93] . Pitchbook provided us with data on AI venture capital and private equity funding for 2016–18 for China, the European Union, and the United States. Pitchbook defines AI firms as those “developing technologies that enable computers to autonomously learn, deduce and act, through utilization of large datasets. The technology enables development of systems that collect and store massive amounts of data, and analyze that content to make decisions based on probability and statistical analysis. Applications for Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning include speech recognition, computer vision, robotic control and accelerating processes in the empirical sciences where large datasets are essential.” Pitchbook’s data demonstrates the United States received 57 percent of venture capital funding going to AI firms in 2018, compared with 29 percent of Chinese firms and 7 percent for EU firms. Pitchbook accessed the data on June 7, 2019.

Daniel Castro is president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), the world’s top-ranked think tank for science and technology policy, where he leads the organization’s work shaping debates on critical issues at the intersection of technological innovation and public policy. He is a prolific writer and respected public speaker on issues ranging from Internet policy and digital governance to artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. Castro also founded and is director of ITIF’s Center for Data Innovation, a leading voice on open data, artificial intelligence, and digital transformation. He has played a key role in advancing the OPEN Government Data Act and has long worked on the policy and economic impact of data-driven innovation. His work on AI spans a broad range of policy issues, including adoption and diffusion, privacy and security, intellectual property, deepfakes and information integrity, and the economic and competitive dynamics of AI, as well as global competition and governance—particularly in China and Europe.

Michael McLaughlin is a research analyst at the Center for Data Innovation. He researches and writes about a variety of issues related to information technology and Internet policy, including digital platforms, e-government, and artificial intelligence. Michael graduated from Wake Forest University, where he majored in Communication with Minors in Politics and International Affairs and Journalism. He received his Master’s in Communication at Stanford University, specializing in Data Journalism.

Eline Chivot is a former senior policy analyst at the Center for Data Innovation. Prior to joining the Center for Data Innovation, Eline Chivot worked for several years in the Netherlands as policy analyst in a leading think tank, where her work included research projects on defense, security and economic policy issues. More recently, Eline worked at one of Brussels’ largest trade associations and managed its relations with representatives of the digital tech industry in Europe and beyond. Eline earned master’s degrees in political science and economics from Sciences Po, and in strategic management and business administration from the University of Lille.

extraction.body: As Washington strives for technological dominance and Beijing builds technological self-sufficiency, the global technology system is splitting. The race for technological superiority between the United States and China requires third countries to sustain the advantages of each great power. Europe has a key role to play in this geopolitical rivalry, but its perceptions and cost-benefit analyses are being reevaluated as the Trump administration’s stance toward the European Union becomes more aggressive. Initiatives to build Europe’s technological sovereignty have proliferated in recent years, and opposition to reliance on U.S. platforms has grown as the United States’ retaliatory and punitive measures have intensified. The costs for Europe of building its own technology stack are considerable, with estimates starting at €3.6 trillion . But the security costs of continued reliance on U.S. technology are equally severe. The United States, for its part, is committed to achieving technological dominance . The Trump Administration’s “AI Action Plan” states that the United States “must meet global demand for AI by exporting its full AI technology stack . . . to all countries willing to join America’s AI alliance.” Yet adversarial measures toward longstanding allies, including Europe and Canada, are pushing those same partners to diversify away from U.S. technology, ultimately undermining Washington’s technological ambitions. U.S. technological dominance must be global, and for it to succeed, it must be coproduced. The United States needs allies to not only absorb its technology but also to help produce the technology––all the more so as technological competition concentrates at the cutting edge. Adversarial behaviors and policies, by contrast, will produce the opposite effect, reducing the incentives to rely on U.S. technology and spurring technological indigenization as well as diversification, including toward China. The United States holds a technologically dominant position relative to Europe. Sensitive European government, health, and corporate data is stored on servers subject to U.S. surveillance laws, such as the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data (CLOUD) Act and the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act . Regulatory control over platforms gives the United States the capacity to retaliate against European policy initiatives it perceives as discriminatory. Cloud access can be deliberately interrupted for political purposes. Europe’s perceptions of U.S. hostility are turning these concerns into a conviction that reliance on U.S. technology poses an existential threat. European governments are actively working to move away from U.S. technology. The Tech Sovereignty Package introduced earlier this year, the Cloud and AI Development Act , and the Chips Act 2.0 are emblematic of this shift. France, meanwhile, has restricted the use of Zoom and Microsoft Teams. France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy have joined forces to build European digital commons . Most commentary on these initiatives has questioned their credibility and feasibility. Indeed, in October 2026, Europe-based search engine Ecosia announced it would drop French AI company Mistral from its backend, instead opting to use cheaper and more capable Chinese alternatives. But Europe’s motivation, and the resources it commits to reducing its dependence on U.S. technology, will grow in proportion to perceived U.S. antagonism. While budget strains might complicate these efforts, if national security is on the line, traditional fiscal orthodoxy is still likely to bend, with efforts to decouple increasing at either the supranational or national level. And while Europeans will undergo a costly process of adjustment, Americans risk losing significant market access that will not automatically be absorbed elsewhere. The result will be a net loss on both sides of the Atlantic. The scale of the transatlantic market is far from negligible. In 2025, U.S.-EU trade was valued at approximately $2 trillion . No other bilateral trade and investment relationship in the world is comparable. The transatlantic economy accounts for almost a third of global trade in goods and services and 43 percent of global GDP . Moreover, the relationship is complementary: In 2025, U.S. goods exports to the European Union totaled $412.5 billion and imports $632.9 billion; in services, U.S. exports amounted to $324.8 billion and imports from the bloc to $217.6 billion. In digital services, Europe is a vital market for U.S. cloud providers. In 2025, the market share of U.S. cloud providers in Europe exceeded 80 percent, compared with around 15 percent for European providers. In artificial intelligence, European model providers struggle to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. Dependencies cut both ways: Europe’s reliance on the United States for technology supplies is mirrored by U.S. tech providers’ reliance on European demand. Moreover, U.S. technology is coproduced with European industry leaders. The case is clearest when it comes to U.S. reliance on Dutch company ASML ’s extreme ultraviolet machines. But ASML is not the only U.S. dependency. ZEISS’s optics and TRUMPF’s lasers are indispensable components of the extreme ultraviolet lithography ecosystem; Imec is a critical hub for advanced semiconductor research and development; Ericsson and Nokia are major suppliers of US 5G and telecommunications infrastructure; and companies such as Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Siemens, and Bosch Rexroth are deeply embedded in U.S. automotive, power-electronics, industrial-automation, AI, and manufacturing supply chains. Concerns about U.S. technology affect European businesses as well as governments. EU-listed companies rely on the United States for almost a fifth of their revenues . Yet partnerships with U.S. counterparts and the use of components and technologies with U.S. content expose private companies to the risk of suddenly being targeted by extraterritorial rules. This creates an unfavorable business environment and dims prospects for profitability, motivating supply chain and market diversification. In a 2025 survey, more German companies said they planned to reduce their investments in the United States than said they planned to increase them. Smaller member states have noted that some prospective first-time investors in the United States have abandoned their plans, while businesses with long-standing U.S. relationships planned to continue to invest. Notably, U.S. policies that make alignment with Washington strategically more costly increase the relative attractiveness of diversification. Since Europe began exploring its options in earnest at the start of the second Trump administration, French President Emmanuel Macron made a state visit to China (widely hailed as a success ), with Chinese President Xi Jinping embracing Europe’s aspirations for strategic autonomy. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s also made a trip to China, accompanied by a delegation of business leaders from Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes, and Siemens, all of whom were seeking contracts. The visit’s objective was to “improve and make fair” Sino-German relations. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney––now in the process of formalizing its association partnership with the European Union––also traveled to China earlier this year to forge a “new strategic partnership with People’s Republic of China.” Given Western concerns over Beijing’s trade practices, such visits send a particularly strong signal to Washington : Traditional allies are willing to hedge their technological dependencies for greater economic security. There is still an opportunity to make the transatlantic relationship the foundation of a larger and more resilient technology ecosystem. Restoring the partnership, however, does not mean restoring the status quo. The future transatlantic technology relationship should rather enable both sides to gain control over sensitive technological bottlenecks, thereby restoring a domestic sense of security, while deepening interdependence in areas where capabilities are difficult to develop domestically or are not critical enough to justify the effort. The United States should encourage greater European participation in the U.S. technology ecosystem, including through government procurement, defense cooperation, and commercial partnerships. Precedents for this model already exist: European defense-tech and telecom companies have secured direct U.S. government contracts and entered into transatlantic teaming arrangements. At the same time, Washington should help foster a positive environment for U.S. firms to participate in EU markets and supply chains. There is an appetite for this. Commenting on Intel’s continued partnership with ASML, Intel’s executive vice president said the company “will continue to work closely with ASML and the entire industry to enable [the AI] transition.” In summer 2026, Paris-based Mistral AI established a strategic cloud distribution and infrastructure partnership with Microsoft, allowing European-developed models to run on U.S. hyperscale computing infrastructure. This is notable, considering the company has long been regarded as Europe’s only AI champion. Such deals, however, will multiply only to the extent that governments and companies on both sides of the Atlantic perceive the business climate as positive. Efforts to renew the partnership should not assume that current tensions will simply disappear. A significant segment of European political opinion hopes that the current period of confrontation will pass, much as the relationship recovered after the first Trump administration. Still, U.S. rapprochement will possibly be met with European resentment: European governments might use recent episodes of U.S. aversion as leverage to extract political advantages from future engagement with the United States. While policies adopted today to reduce dependence on the United States could be softened in a period of rapprochement, however, they may still become embedded in Europe’s emerging industrial policy. History points this direction: France’s departure from NATO’s integrated command in 1966 did not end the alliance, but the defense-industrial and nuclear autonomy France built in those years outlasted the rupture by decades. The more plausible outcome, then, is that cooperation will resume on terms that preserve space for European autonomy. If the United States wants Europe to remain part of a U.S.-led technological ecosystem, it needs to make participation the more attractive option for European governments. The United States cannot compete with China while losing its allies. Meeting the China challenge requires building an ecosystem capable of achieving the same scale and offering countries around the world a credible alternative. Europe is indispensable to that effort. Its markets and industrial capabilities sustain the attractiveness and resilience of U.S. technology and enable the United States to shape the next generation of technology. For the United States to win the technology race and establish technological dominance vis-à-vis China, it must first make sure its allies remain in the race with it. This would require Washington to move away from leveraging Europe’s technological dependencies and toward offering Europe a stake in coproducing the technologies of the future, through more open procurement, joint investment, and commitments capable of enduring across administrations. Federico Steinberg is a visiting fellow with the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C. Riccardo Bosticco is a PhD researcher at the Centre for Security, Diplomacy and Strategy at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and Fulbright visiting researcher at Georgetown University School of Foreign Service. The race for technological superiority between the United States and China requires third countries to sustain the advantages of each great power. Europe has a key role to play in this geopolitical rivalry, but its perceptions and cost-benefit analyses are being reevaluated as the Trump administration’s stance toward the European Union becomes more aggressive.

Initiatives to build Europe’s technological sovereignty have proliferated in recent years, and opposition to reliance on U.S. platforms has grown as the United States’ retaliatory and punitive measures have intensified. The costs for Europe of building its own technology stack are considerable, with estimates starting at €3.6 trillion . But the security costs of continued reliance on U.S. technology are equally severe.

The United States, for its part, is committed to achieving technological dominance . The Trump Administration’s “AI Action Plan” states that the United States “must meet global demand for AI by exporting its full AI technology stack . . . to all countries willing to join America’s AI alliance.” Yet adversarial measures toward longstanding allies, including Europe and Canada, are pushing those same partners to diversify away from U.S. technology, ultimately undermining Washington’s technological ambitions.

U.S. technological dominance must be global, and for it to succeed, it must be coproduced. The United States needs allies to not only absorb its technology but also to help produce the technology––all the more so as technological competition concentrates at the cutting edge. Adversarial behaviors and policies, by contrast, will produce the opposite effect, reducing the incentives to rely on U.S. technology and spurring technological indigenization as well as diversification, including toward China.

The United States holds a technologically dominant position relative to Europe. Sensitive European government, health, and corporate data is stored on servers subject to U.S. surveillance laws, such as the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data (CLOUD) Act and the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act . Regulatory control over platforms gives the United States the capacity to retaliate against European policy initiatives it perceives as discriminatory. Cloud access can be deliberately interrupted for political purposes. Europe’s perceptions of U.S. hostility are turning these concerns into a conviction that reliance on U.S. technology poses an existential threat.

European governments are actively working to move away from U.S. technology. The Tech Sovereignty Package introduced earlier this year, the Cloud and AI Development Act , and the Chips Act 2.0 are emblematic of this shift. France, meanwhile, has restricted the use of Zoom and Microsoft Teams. France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy have joined forces to build European digital commons .

Most commentary on these initiatives has questioned their credibility and feasibility. Indeed, in October 2026, Europe-based search engine Ecosia announced it would drop French AI company Mistral from its backend, instead opting to use cheaper and more capable Chinese alternatives. But Europe’s motivation, and the resources it commits to reducing its dependence on U.S. technology, will grow in proportion to perceived U.S. antagonism. While budget strains might complicate these efforts, if national security is on the line, traditional fiscal orthodoxy is still likely to bend, with efforts to decouple increasing at either the supranational or national level. And while Europeans will undergo a costly process of adjustment, Americans risk losing significant market access that will not automatically be absorbed elsewhere. The result will be a net loss on both sides of the Atlantic.

The scale of the transatlantic market is far from negligible. In 2025, U.S.-EU trade was valued at approximately $2 trillion . No other bilateral trade and investment relationship in the world is comparable. The transatlantic economy accounts for almost a third of global trade in goods and services and 43 percent of global GDP . Moreover, the relationship is complementary: In 2025, U.S. goods exports to the European Union totaled $412.5 billion and imports $632.9 billion; in services, U.S. exports amounted to $324.8 billion and imports from the bloc to $217.6 billion.

In digital services, Europe is a vital market for U.S. cloud providers. In 2025, the market share of U.S. cloud providers in Europe exceeded 80 percent, compared with around 15 percent for European providers. In artificial intelligence, European model providers struggle to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. Dependencies cut both ways: Europe’s reliance on the United States for technology supplies is mirrored by U.S. tech providers’ reliance on European demand.

Moreover, U.S. technology is coproduced with European industry leaders. The case is clearest when it comes to U.S. reliance on Dutch company ASML ’s extreme ultraviolet machines. But ASML is not the only U.S. dependency. ZEISS’s optics and TRUMPF’s lasers are indispensable components of the extreme ultraviolet lithography ecosystem; Imec is a critical hub for advanced semiconductor research and development; Ericsson and Nokia are major suppliers of US 5G and telecommunications infrastructure; and companies such as Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Siemens, and Bosch Rexroth are deeply embedded in U.S. automotive, power-electronics, industrial-automation, AI, and manufacturing supply chains.

Concerns about U.S. technology affect European businesses as well as governments. EU-listed companies rely on the United States for almost a fifth of their revenues . Yet partnerships with U.S. counterparts and the use of components and technologies with U.S. content expose private companies to the risk of suddenly being targeted by extraterritorial rules. This creates an unfavorable business environment and dims prospects for profitability, motivating supply chain and market diversification. In a 2025 survey, more German companies said they planned to reduce their investments in the United States than said they planned to increase them. Smaller member states have noted that some prospective first-time investors in the United States have abandoned their plans, while businesses with long-standing U.S. relationships planned to continue to invest.

Notably, U.S. policies that make alignment with Washington strategically more costly increase the relative attractiveness of diversification. Since Europe began exploring its options in earnest at the start of the second Trump administration, French President Emmanuel Macron made a state visit to China (widely hailed as a success ), with Chinese President Xi Jinping embracing Europe’s aspirations for strategic autonomy. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s also made a trip to China, accompanied by a delegation of business leaders from Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes, and Siemens, all of whom were seeking contracts. The visit’s objective was to “improve and make fair” Sino-German relations. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney––now in the process of formalizing its association partnership with the European Union––also traveled to China earlier this year to forge a “new strategic partnership with People’s Republic of China.” Given Western concerns over Beijing’s trade practices, such visits send a particularly strong signal to Washington : Traditional allies are willing to hedge their technological dependencies for greater economic security.

There is still an opportunity to make the transatlantic relationship the foundation of a larger and more resilient technology ecosystem. Restoring the partnership, however, does not mean restoring the status quo. The future transatlantic technology relationship should rather enable both sides to gain control over sensitive technological bottlenecks, thereby restoring a domestic sense of security, while deepening interdependence in areas where capabilities are difficult to develop domestically or are not critical enough to justify the effort.

The United States should encourage greater European participation in the U.S. technology ecosystem, including through government procurement, defense cooperation, and commercial partnerships. Precedents for this model already exist: European defense-tech and telecom companies have secured direct U.S. government contracts and entered into transatlantic teaming arrangements.

At the same time, Washington should help foster a positive environment for U.S. firms to participate in EU markets and supply chains. There is an appetite for this. Commenting on Intel’s continued partnership with ASML, Intel’s executive vice president said the company “will continue to work closely with ASML and the entire industry to enable [the AI] transition.” In summer 2026, Paris-based Mistral AI established a strategic cloud distribution and infrastructure partnership with Microsoft, allowing European-developed models to run on U.S. hyperscale computing infrastructure. This is notable, considering the company has long been regarded as Europe’s only AI champion.

Such deals, however, will multiply only to the extent that governments and companies on both sides of the Atlantic perceive the business climate as positive. Efforts to renew the partnership should not assume that current tensions will simply disappear. A significant segment of European political opinion hopes that the current period of confrontation will pass, much as the relationship recovered after the first Trump administration. Still, U.S. rapprochement will possibly be met with European resentment: European governments might use recent episodes of U.S. aversion as leverage to extract political advantages from future engagement with the United States.

While policies adopted today to reduce dependence on the United States could be softened in a period of rapprochement, however, they may still become embedded in Europe’s emerging industrial policy. History points this direction: France’s departure from NATO’s integrated command in 1966 did not end the alliance, but the defense-industrial and nuclear autonomy France built in those years outlasted the rupture by decades.
The more plausible outcome, then, is that cooperation will resume on terms that preserve space for European autonomy.
If the United States wants Europe to remain part of a U.S.-led technological ecosystem, it needs to make participation the more attractive option for European governments.

The United States cannot compete with China while losing its allies. Meeting the China challenge requires building an ecosystem capable of achieving the same scale and offering countries around the world a credible alternative. Europe is indispensable to that effort. Its markets and industrial capabilities sustain the attractiveness and resilience of U.S. technology and enable the United States to shape the next generation of technology.

For the United States to win the technology race and establish technological dominance vis-à-vis China, it must first make sure its allies remain in the race with it. This would require Washington to move away from leveraging Europe’s technological dependencies and toward offering Europe a stake in coproducing the technologies of the future, through more open procurement, joint investment, and commitments capable of enduring across administrations.

Federico Steinberg is a visiting fellow with the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C. Riccardo Bosticco is a PhD researcher at the Centre for Security, Diplomacy and Strategy at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and Fulbright visiting researcher at Georgetown University School of Foreign Service.

sources.title: As data centers remain potent political issue, David Crowley offers plan to regulate artificial intelligence in Wisconsin
passages: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.

Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.
Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025.
The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action.
Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13. Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors. Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors. Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders. More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. extraction.body: NEW YORK — The NFL will have "heightened" security measures around the Saints-Steelers game scheduled to be played Sunday in Paris amid the civil unrest and violence occurring in France, a top league executive said Tuesday. "Our team's been on the ground," said Peter O'Reilly, the NFL's executive vice president of club business, international, and league events. "Our security team's been on the ground and obviously working in close partnership with Stade de France, which is a world-class stadium, hosted world-class events. … But not just on game day. Paris Saint-Germain played Barcelona in a Champions League match Tuesday without incident. The soccer club plays at Parc des Princes, closer to the urban core, while the NFL game will be at the Stade de France in suburban Saint-Dennis. At least seven Saints players were at the soccer game Tuesday. "All of our events we have going on … we always have a very strong security presence, as you know, around all of those events," O'Reilly said. "And that presence will be heightened, with local authorities making sure that there's nothing more important from our standpoint that team security, fan security, everybody involved with this game. So extremely vigilant, as we always are. But, as I said, confident in all of those plans as we head toward Sunday." O'Reilly spoke at a news conference on the opening day of a two-day meeting of the NFL's team owners at a Manhattan hotel. "All of our plans for the Paris game this weekend are moving forward as planned," he said. "We're confident in our operational and security plans. Our team's been on the ground there for about 10 days." The NFL has not given serious consideration to moving or postponing the game, O'Reilly said. "We have never been close to that point," he said. The NFL will vigorously defend its suspensions of two game officials imposed this month for on-field incidents involving players , the league's top football executive said Tuesday. The NFL Referees Association said earlier this month that it would contest those suspensions . The NFLRA called the league's suspensions of line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one game "excessive and inconsistent with past precedent." But Troy Vincent, the NFL's executive vice president of football operations, said Tuesday: "We deal with the consequence of the grievance. We're going to fight that to the very end. And we feel like we resolved it. It's hey, they sat. Adrian returned back this week. Jeff's still out. But those are: You crossed the line. So that's really, frankly, a non-negotiable." Seeman was involved in a verbal exchange with Cardinals tight end Trey McBride following a fourth-quarter play during an Arizona game against the Giants at MetLife Stadium. McBride was on the sideline when Seeman was caught on camera appearing to curse at the tight end. Officials did not call a penalty on a Giants defender on the play. It was not clear what McBride said to Seeman. During a Dolphins-Vikings game, Hill gestured and appeared to yell at Minnesota linebacker Eric Wilson after being knocked to the ground by Wilson on a play that was whistled dead because of a penalty. Wilson was being blocked by a Miami player, and his contact with Hill appeared inadvertent. "That's just unacceptable," Vincent said Tuesday. "Our team's been on the ground," said Peter O'Reilly, the NFL's executive vice president of club business, international, and league events. "Our security team's been on the ground and obviously working in close partnership with Stade de France, which is a world-class stadium, hosted world-class events. … But not just on game day. Paris Saint-Germain played Barcelona in a Champions League match Tuesday without incident. The soccer club plays at Parc des Princes, closer to the urban core, while the NFL game will be at the Stade de France in suburban Saint-Dennis. At least seven Saints players were at the soccer game Tuesday. "All of our events we have going on … we always have a very strong security presence, as you know, around all of those events," O'Reilly said. "And that presence will be heightened, with local authorities making sure that there's nothing more important from our standpoint that team security, fan security, everybody involved with this game. So extremely vigilant, as we always are. But, as I said, confident in all of those plans as we head toward Sunday." O'Reilly spoke at a news conference on the opening day of a two-day meeting of the NFL's team owners at a Manhattan hotel. "All of our plans for the Paris game this weekend are moving forward as planned," he said. "We're confident in our operational and security plans. Our team's been on the ground there for about 10 days." The NFL has not given serious consideration to moving or postponing the game, O'Reilly said. "We have never been close to that point," he said. The NFL will vigorously defend its suspensions of two game officials imposed this month for on-field incidents involving players , the league's top football executive said Tuesday. The NFL Referees Association said earlier this month that it would contest those suspensions . The NFLRA called the league's suspensions of line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one game "excessive and inconsistent with past precedent." But Troy Vincent, the NFL's executive vice president of football operations, said Tuesday: "We deal with the consequence of the grievance. We're going to fight that to the very end. And we feel like we resolved it. It's hey, they sat. Adrian returned back this week. Jeff's still out. But those are: You crossed the line. So that's really, frankly, a non-negotiable." Seeman was involved in a verbal exchange with Cardinals tight end Trey McBride following a fourth-quarter play during an Arizona game against the Giants at MetLife Stadium. McBride was on the sideline when Seeman was caught on camera appearing to curse at the tight end. Officials did not call a penalty on a Giants defender on the play. It was not clear what McBride said to Seeman. During a Dolphins-Vikings game, Hill gestured and appeared to yell at Minnesota linebacker Eric Wilson after being knocked to the ground by Wilson on a play that was whistled dead because of a penalty. Wilson was being blocked by a Miami player, and his contact with Hill appeared inadvertent. "That's just unacceptable," Vincent said Tuesday. extraction.body: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.

To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song.

Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said.

“That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said.

Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said.
The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said.

The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network.

Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more.
Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry.
Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said.
“This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.”

(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term capital market assumptions for the first time, forecasting returns that could beat stocks, bonds and gold in a milestone for its Wall Street acceptance.
The firm stops short of incorporating Bitcoin into its main portfolio models, it said in a report this week, citing its unstable correlations with other assets.

The JPMorgan analysts say that even as many investors see Bitcoin as a speculative asset, they're still exploring cryptocurrencies — a tenth of clients recently surveyed said their portfolios held crypto, and roughly 17% said they planned to "prioritize crypto." That's thanks, in part, to a regulatory framework that has become more developed and better defined.
But there's a catch: Bitcoin's extreme volatility threatens to undermine its appeal on a risk-adjusted basis.

passages: Major UK banks are blocking or restricting customers' transfers to crypto platforms, with more than 10,000 complaints filed over a three-month period.
Banks that impose transfer limits received 6,198 complaints, while those without a published policy restricting crypto transfers received 2,842.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY) received the most complaints, at 2,297, followed by Barclays (LON: BARC) with 1,569 and NatWest Group (LON: NWG) with 1,278.
Lloyds, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, accounted for more than 22% of the total complaints.
The complaints involved all major UK retail banks and came from every one of the country's 650 parliamentary constituencies.
HSBC UK (LSE: HSBA) and Monzo were also among the banks named in the report, which found that restrictions were not limited to institutions with explicit crypto bans.

Stand With Crypto said the figures suggest customers cannot reliably predict whether their bank will allow them to transfer money to regulated crypto platforms, even when the bank does not publicly prohibit such payments.

sources.title: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys - Decrypt
passages: Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

extraction.body: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards. Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.” The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections. Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit. Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.” The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022. Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 . In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account. Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card. passages: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys
Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

passages: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys
Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”
