extraction.body: Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime. “They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch. In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.” Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to 10 years ago. Take a look for yourself: What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?” When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch. These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks , say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point. “Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.” Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. “Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.” Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California–Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gig workers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them. “What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues. Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models — the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks — aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones. The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it. “Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.” Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real. “What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.” Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms. “What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.” Buy One Pass, Get a Second Free Cover more ground at TechCrunch’s ultimate founder bootcamp of the year by bringing your co-founder or partner for free Book before the BOGO deal expires People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again Sarah Perez Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings Anthony Ha Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says Kirsten Korosec Lucas Ropek Rebecca Bellan Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept Connie Loizos India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity Aditya Mehta Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style Sean O'Kane

extraction.body: Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime. “They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch. In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.” Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to 10 years ago. Take a look for yourself: What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?” When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch. These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks , say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point. “Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.” Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes. “Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.” Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California–Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gig workers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them. “What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues. Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models — the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks — aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones. The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.

“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”

Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.

“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”

passages: Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year.
It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however.
The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League.
It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers.
CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage.
Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

passages: SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however.
The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League.
It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers.
CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage.
Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing . That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition. The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company. The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter. During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online. “People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity. Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million. passages: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor.
To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air.

And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.
They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards.
Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park.
They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments.
Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes .

extraction.body: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

extraction.body: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

extraction.body: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” [Video: Personal Intelligence in cars] Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

passages: Get hands-free personalized help on the road with Gemini
Gemini is now available on Android Auto and cars with Google built-in, offering a hands-free way to manage tasks while driving.
You can now enable Personal Intelligence to let Gemini pull information from your emails, photos, and calendar to provide tailored answers to complex questions.
To get started, check your Gemini settings to opt in and connect your preferred apps.
An assistant is even more helpful when it knows the world and knows you.
With Gemini, you can speak naturally to get more done or brainstorm ideas while driving.
If you've already enabled it in the Gemini app, it comes with you into the car.
You’re in total control of your privacy, so you can choose exactly what information Gemini can access.
We built Personal Intelligence with privacy at the center .
Personal Intelligence has two core strengths: retrieving specific details from, say, an email, photo or a place you saved in Google Maps to answer your question and reasoning across complex sources.

Personal Intelligence is currently rolling out to eligible personal Google accounts (and not for Workspace business, enterprise, or education users) aged 18 and older globally, excluding the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and Nigeria.

sources.title: Gemini can now draw on your Google data to personalize the images it generates - Engadget
passages: Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini.

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model.

Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context.

Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead.
Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

extraction.body: Your Google data can act as an extra reference point for Nano Banana 2. Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini. After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

extraction.body: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products. The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said. That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said. Your prompts and commands don’t have to include specifics as Personal Intelligence can pull those details from emails, photos, or a “place you saved in Google Maps.” This allows for complex or natural queries, like “What’s my flight gate? And is my flight on time?” or “Take me to my doctor’s appointment.” Additionally, Gemini is aware of your preferences when you say: “Find me an indoor restaurant along my route that matches my usual vibe.” This saves you from having to specify you’re vegetarian with every command. On the privacy front, Personal Intelligence is opt-in, though it will come to Android Auto automatically if you enabled it for the Gemini app on your phone. If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you. Meanwhile, on Android Automotive, Personal Intelligence will only share personalized responses “when you’re in the car with your phone connected.” Personal Intelligence is rolling out starting today to Android Auto, with Android Automotive availability in the coming months. extraction.body: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products. The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle. The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed. Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said. That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said. extraction.body: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” [Video: Personal Intelligence in cars] Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. extraction.body: Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” [Video: Personal Intelligence in cars] Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps. Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says. Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

sources.title: Oracle posts 30% revenue growth fueled by AI cloud demand as debts hits $125 billion - CNBC
passages: Oracle shares whipsawed on Friday after the software company reported 30% revenue growth for the latest quarter, topping estimates, with sales fueled by strong demand for cloud infrastructure.
Alongside selling its flagship database software, Oracle now has $125 billion in debt as it funds an expansive buildout of data centers for AI workloads.
The investment is expected to expand capacity for contracted cloud demand from customers including Nvidia, Meta, OpenAI, Advanced Micro Devices and SpaceX's AI business.
The company guided to second-quarter revenue growth of 30% to 34%, with cloud revenue rising between 64% and 70%.
It expects total revenue for the 2027 fiscal year to be at least $90 billion.
Oracle delivered an additional 850 megawatts of data center capacity in the quarter.
It also booked over $30 billion in further AI cloud contracts, and delivered more than 300,000 graphics processing units to its AI Cloud customers.
Oracle posted $5.4 billion in negative free cash flow during the quarter, versus a negative $362 million a year earlier.
Oracle's outlook for 2027 is "modest," and the company's management framework is "conservative," the analysts said.
WATCH: Oracle shares spike on earnings and revenue
Fiscal first-quarter revenue increased to $19.35 billion, beating LSEG consensus estimates of $19.14 billion.
Even with Friday's rally, Oracle is down about 20% this year on concern about the hefty amount of debt the company has raised to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
Citi analysts reiterated their buy rating in a Friday note, saying Oracle had met expectations and "cleared the runway" for its upcoming investor day.

extraction.body: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity. Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity, and super intelligence,” CEO Elon Musk declared at the start of the earnings call, held live from the company’s Starlink factory in Bastrop, Texas. The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute. The SI segment alone generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up $5 billion quarter-over-quarter and $6.7 billion year-over-year, fueled by the ramp of cloud services agreements and the mid-quarter acquisition of Cursor. Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year. Space segment revenue reached $1.8 billion, up 84% sequentially but only 6% year-over-year, reflecting a favorable customer mix. SpaceX launched 35 rockets in Q3, including 21 Starlink Falcon 9 missions, two Starship flights, one Falcon Heavy, and 12 customer missions. The company secured 18 new national security space launch missions and three additional human spaceflight missions on Dragon. Connectivity revenue rose 69% year-over-year and 22% sequentially to $5.2 billion. Starlink consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million, adding 1.6 million in the quarter. Monthly ARPU increased 5% sequentially to $69. Enterprise and government revenue jumped 91% year-over-year, highlighted by Starshield and aviation contracts now covering roughly 12,000 planes—nearly a quarter of the available aircraft worldwide. “Starlink is now contracted for roughly 12,000 planes, almost a quarter of the available aircraft,” said CFO Gwynne Shotwell, adding that Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa Airlines, Korean Air, Austrian Airlines, and Asiana Airlines all flew their first Starlink-equipped aircraft during the quarter. Starlink Mobile surpassed 22 million monthly users, up 37% quarter-over-quarter. The company also received FCC approval to launch 15,000 mobile V2 satellites and announced an agreement to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum. SI segment revenue of $7.6 billion included $608 million from Cursor, which closed mid-quarter. Excluding Cursor, SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially, driven primarily by the activation of new cloud services agreements. SI segment adjusted EBITDA was $5 billion, up $3.8 billion quarter-over-quarter. Operating income was $431 million; excluding $1.2 billion in stock-based compensation from Cursor, operating profit was $1.6 billion. “We ended the third quarter with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity, with additional data halls already online in early October,” said Brad Garlinghouse, CFO. “We expect to have nearly 2 gigawatts by the end of October and 2.5-3 gigawatts by the end of the fourth quarter.” The company noted that new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year at current pricing, which is tracking slightly above the high end of the $30-$50 per watt range discussed last quarter. SpaceX launched Starship Flight 14 in the final week of the quarter, which reached orbit and deployed operational Starlink V3 satellites—a key milestone. Flight 15, scheduled for November, will attempt to catch both the booster and the ship. “If we succeed, it will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered,” Musk said. “This is a massive technology milestone. The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle.” Musk also announced the Louisiana Spaceport, targeting first launch in 2028 with high confidence in 2029. The company expects Starship to fly weekly in the first half of 2027 and twice weekly or more by the end of 2027. For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts. He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity, and super intelligence,” CEO Elon Musk declared at the start of the earnings call, held live from the company’s Starlink factory in Bastrop, Texas.

The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute. The SI segment alone generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up $5 billion quarter-over-quarter and $6.7 billion year-over-year, fueled by the ramp of cloud services agreements and the mid-quarter acquisition of Cursor.
Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year.

Space segment revenue reached $1.8 billion, up 84% sequentially but only 6% year-over-year, reflecting a favorable customer mix. SpaceX launched 35 rockets in Q3, including 21 Starlink Falcon 9 missions, two Starship flights, one Falcon Heavy, and 12 customer missions. The company secured 18 new national security space launch missions and three additional human spaceflight missions on Dragon.

Connectivity revenue rose 69% year-over-year and 22% sequentially to $5.2 billion. Starlink consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million, adding 1.6 million in the quarter. Monthly ARPU increased 5% sequentially to $69. Enterprise and government revenue jumped 91% year-over-year, highlighted by Starshield and aviation contracts now covering roughly 12,000 planes—nearly a quarter of the available aircraft worldwide.

“Starlink is now contracted for roughly 12,000 planes, almost a quarter of the available aircraft,” said CFO Gwynne Shotwell, adding that Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa Airlines, Korean Air, Austrian Airlines, and Asiana Airlines all flew their first Starlink-equipped aircraft during the quarter.

Starlink Mobile surpassed 22 million monthly users, up 37% quarter-over-quarter. The company also received FCC approval to launch 15,000 mobile V2 satellites and announced an agreement to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum.

SI segment revenue of $7.6 billion included $608 million from Cursor, which closed mid-quarter. Excluding Cursor, SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially, driven primarily by the activation of new cloud services agreements. SI segment adjusted EBITDA was $5 billion, up $3.8 billion quarter-over-quarter. Operating income was $431 million; excluding $1.2 billion in stock-based compensation from Cursor, operating profit was $1.6 billion.

The company noted that new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year at current pricing, which is tracking slightly above the high end of the $30-$50 per watt range discussed last quarter.

“If we succeed, it will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered,” Musk said. “This is a massive technology milestone. The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle.”

No agreement on terms has been reached.

She expects S-band spectrum to carry the majority of traffic, with low-band spectrum providing critical building penetration. Musk added that the company sees a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue and will detail the plan in a future presentation.

extraction.body: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) delivered a blowout third quarter of 2026, with revenue surging 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, driven by an inflection in its Super Intelligence (SI) segment and continued momentum in Starlink connectivity. Net income swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA more than quadrupled to $8.8 billion. “We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity, and super intelligence,” CEO Elon Musk declared at the start of the earnings call, held live from the company’s Starlink factory in Bastrop, Texas. The results underscore SpaceX’s transformation from a pure-play launch provider into a diversified technology platform spanning space infrastructure, satellite broadband, and AI compute. The SI segment alone generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up $5 billion quarter-over-quarter and $6.7 billion year-over-year, fueled by the ramp of cloud services agreements and the mid-quarter acquisition of Cursor. Source: Company earnings release; backlog includes $17.5B deferred revenue, with ~$42B expected to be recognized within the next year. Space segment revenue reached $1.8 billion, up 84% sequentially but only 6% year-over-year, reflecting a favorable customer mix. SpaceX launched 35 rockets in Q3, including 21 Starlink Falcon 9 missions, two Starship flights, one Falcon Heavy, and 12 customer missions. The company secured 18 new national security space launch missions and three additional human spaceflight missions on Dragon. Connectivity revenue rose 69% year-over-year and 22% sequentially to $5.2 billion. Starlink consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million, adding 1.6 million in the quarter. Monthly ARPU increased 5% sequentially to $69. Enterprise and government revenue jumped 91% year-over-year, highlighted by Starshield and aviation contracts now covering roughly 12,000 planes—nearly a quarter of the available aircraft worldwide. “Starlink is now contracted for roughly 12,000 planes, almost a quarter of the available aircraft,” said CFO Gwynne Shotwell, adding that Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa Airlines, Korean Air, Austrian Airlines, and Asiana Airlines all flew their first Starlink-equipped aircraft during the quarter. Starlink Mobile surpassed 22 million monthly users, up 37% quarter-over-quarter. The company also received FCC approval to launch 15,000 mobile V2 satellites and announced an agreement to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum. SI segment revenue of $7.6 billion included $608 million from Cursor, which closed mid-quarter. Excluding Cursor, SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially, driven primarily by the activation of new cloud services agreements. SI segment adjusted EBITDA was $5 billion, up $3.8 billion quarter-over-quarter. Operating income was $431 million; excluding $1.2 billion in stock-based compensation from Cursor, operating profit was $1.6 billion. “We ended the third quarter with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity, with additional data halls already online in early October,” said Brad Garlinghouse, CFO. “We expect to have nearly 2 gigawatts by the end of October and 2.5-3 gigawatts by the end of the fourth quarter.” The company noted that new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year at current pricing, which is tracking slightly above the high end of the $30-$50 per watt range discussed last quarter. SpaceX launched Starship Flight 14 in the final week of the quarter, which reached orbit and deployed operational Starlink V3 satellites—a key milestone. Flight 15, scheduled for November, will attempt to catch both the booster and the ship. “If we succeed, it will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered,” Musk said. “This is a massive technology milestone. The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle.” Musk also announced the Louisiana Spaceport, targeting first launch in 2028 with high confidence in 2029. The company expects Starship to fly weekly in the first half of 2027 and twice weekly or more by the end of 2027. For 2027, Musk expressed high confidence in adding 10 gigawatts of incremental compute, with a stretch goal of over 20 gigawatts. He also projected SpaceX annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, contingent on SI compute scaling. On Terafab and chip fabrication: Musk said internal expectations are for a first test chip to be functional around May or June 2027 at the Austin research fab, with volume production targeted for Q3 2028 at Terafab in Gibbons Creek. “These are very aggressive dates,” he acknowledged, thanking ASML and other suppliers for accelerating equipment deliveries. On power constraints and funding: Musk revealed that SpaceX is currently turning on 220,000 GB300s per month and has a proprietary plan to reach 20 gigawatts of incremental power and cooling by end-2027. “If you just look at the rate at which we are actually deploying and turning on compute, I’m being as precise as possible about this,” he said. “It is absolutely insane to be deploying, providing the power and all the electrical equipment, the cooling, the batteries, the networking, and everything else that’s needed to turn on 220,000 GB300s a month.” Garlinghouse added that the company has an investment-grade balance sheet and multiple debt capital pools available. On a potential Tesla merger: Musk addressed the long-rumored combination, stating that both companies have formed special committees of independent directors. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. “Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes. At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.” He noted that any deal would require a 50% vote of all Tesla shares, a high hurdle. No agreement on terms has been reached. On Starlink Mobile: Shotwell noted that 85-93% of mobile connectivity is via Wi-Fi and that Starlink broadband supports that. She expects S-band spectrum to carry the majority of traffic, with low-band spectrum providing critical building penetration. Musk added that the company sees a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue and will detail the plan in a future presentation. On compute allocation: Musk said the goal is roughly a 50/50 split between internal and external compute use, with flexibility to shift 60/40 either way. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone,” he said. “That is why I posted that video meme of the Monty Python Cheese Shop sketch, where the guy goes into a cheese shop to get some cheese, and they actually have no cheese.” He added that short-term contracts are renewing at higher dollars per watt, and that a six-month payback period for compute next year is not impossible. On V3 satellite capacity: Shotwell said a few hundred V3 satellites are needed for users to really feel the impact, and she expects to achieve that by mid-2027. On Louisiana Spaceport: Musk said the internal aspiration for first launch from Louisiana is 2028, with 2029 highly likely for at-scale launches. “I’m highly confident,” he said. SpaceX’s Q3 results reflect a company firing on all cylinders, with the SI segment emerging as its largest and fastest-growing business. The aggressive capital expenditure plans and ambitious revenue targets underscore management’s conviction in the AI compute opportunity. However, the capital-intensive nature of the build-out, potential execution challenges in chip fabrication and power infrastructure, and the high hurdle for a Tesla merger remain key risks. For now, investors are likely to focus on the massive revenue guidance for Q1 2027 and the company’s ability to scale compute capacity at an unprecedented pace. passages: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday.

Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call.
OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind.
Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other.
OpenAI says the combined team will build agents that connect scientific findings with the decisions and follow-up studies needed to turn a promising result into an actual medicine.
Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists.
In April, OpenAI launched GPT-Rosalind , a model built specifically for biology and drug discovery, and restricted it to vetted U.S. enterprise customers such as Amgen and Moderna.
In January alone, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health , which lets users connect their medical records to the chatbot, and bought records startup Torch for a reported $100 million to build it out.

Anthropic, OpenAI's closest rival, has been running the same play: it bought AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April and launched a research platform called Claude Science in June.

extraction.body: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday. "Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner," OpenAI said in the announcement. Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists. The financial terms were not disclosed. Getting a new medicine from first idea to U.S. approval takes time—up to 15 years according to OpenAI. Every month shaved off that timeline is a month earlier that a new treatment can reach the people waiting for it, and a month earlier that the company can generate cash. The process is also absurdly expensive: bringing one approved drug to market can cost more than $2.6 billion, and fewer than 10% of candidates that enter human testing ever make it to pharmacy shelves. Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other. Those partners usually include contract research organizations, the outside labs hired to run studies, and contract manufacturers that produce the experimental drug. Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call. Founded in the fall of 2022, Orchestra raised its seed round from Andreessen Horowitz, Definition Capital, Insight Partners, and 8VC, and about $20 million in total, according to Caplight data. The company should not be confused with Orchestra BioMed, an unrelated Nasdaq-listed medical device maker that trades under the ticker OBIO. In April, OpenAI launched GPT-Rosalind , a model built specifically for biology and drug discovery, and restricted it to vetted U.S. enterprise customers such as Amgen and Moderna. A companion product, Rosalind Workbench, connects the model to scientific tools and data so researchers can analyze results and plan experiments. Rosalind helps scientists figure out what to test; Orchestra is supposed to handle what comes after. OpenAI says the combined team will build agents that connect scientific findings with the decisions and follow-up studies needed to turn a promising result into an actual medicine. In January alone, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health , which lets users connect their medical records to the chatbot, and bought records startup Torch for a reported $100 million to build it out. That same month, it turned another acquisition, a scientific writing tool called Crixet, into its Prism platform for researchers. OpenAI Rolls Out Free Science Platform Prism as Experts Warn of Privacy Concerns OpenAI has been upfront that it wants more than subscription fees out of science. In a January blog post, CFO Sarah Friar wrote that as AI moves into drug discovery and similar fields, licensing, IP-based agreements and outcome-based pricing will share in the value created—a polite way of saying OpenAI would like a cut if its tools help produce a blockbuster. Anthropic, OpenAI's closest rival, has been running the same play: it bought AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April and launched a research platform called Claude Science in June. In September, Anthropic said its Claude model helped uncover a previously unknown enzyme system resembling CRISPR, the gene-editing tool, though some scientists said the finding was overblown. OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind. Its previous Rosalind announcement came just five days earlier, when it offered eligible U.S. university labs up to 30 free seats for as long as 12 months through a new Rosalind Academic Plan.

passages: OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI announced the acquisition on October 20, 2026. OpenAI said its goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work required to turn those discoveries into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine takes roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery through regulatory approval in the United States, according to the company, and the teams behind those programs must coordinate work across internal departments and external partners, often through disconnected systems. OpenAI describes the present moment as an inflection point at which AI can take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind is OpenAI’s life sciences brand. OpenAI describes GPT-Rosalind as a purpose-built model that helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry, and Rosalind Workbench as the layer that connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data so researchers can analyze results and plan experiments. Orchestra adds a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. OpenAI said that together the organizations aim to build agents that connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio built its platform around a model in which people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, which OpenAI says frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. According to OpenAI, a problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others: a failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents pinpoint the activities and timelines a problem touches, pull together the relevant information, and compare response options, and scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Orchestra Bio confirmed the acquisition on its own website, saying it started the company four years earlier to help biotech and pharma teams advance their drug development programs. The company describes medicine development as involving thousands of decisions and dependencies that run across discovery, preclinical, manufacturing, and clinical work. In its framing, agents can take on planning, orchestration, and analysis, leaving scientists and program leaders to concentrate on the decisions that require their expertise. Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters. Rosalind Workbench is in research preview, with an orchestrated set of scientific tools connected in a single workspace. It offers an Explore mode for general scientific questions, using the latest ChatGPT models available to the user, and a Research mode that applies GPT-Rosalind to more complex biological questions, in-depth analysis, and advanced research workflows, with access through an application process. Researchers can also use GPT-Rosalind inside Codex to connect their scientific tools, data, and evidence into research workflows that teams can review, share, and reuse, while a GPT-Rosalind API targets organizations that want to integrate life sciences reasoning into their own research applications, internal tools, and governed workflows. API access is subject to eligibility review and organizational approval. OpenAI’s product page reports benchmark results for the model on life sciences research tasks, stated as increases in performance per token: 53.7% on Genebench, 18.0% on Medchem Bench, 19.6% on Labworkbench, and 4.42% on LifeSci Bench. The page lists supported uses that include prioritizing biological targets, engineering proteins, synthesizing evidence across papers and experiments, analyzing unstructured experimental results, and saving workflows that teams can inspect, share, and reuse. OpenAI said its partnership with Novo Nordisk is aimed at translating the drugmaker’s scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance, and that at Moderna, AI is helping teams turn insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. In a statement carried on OpenAI’s Rosalind page , Mike Doustdar, Novo Nordisk’s CEO and president, said: “Our partnership with OpenAI will help translate this scale into faster R&D and commercial execution, while maintaining the governance our patients and society expect.” OpenAI also lists structured access routes beyond enterprise customers. The Rosalind Academic Plan offers eligible labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery. An enterprise option brings GPT-Rosalind into approved research workflows with governance review and enterprise-grade deployment controls, while government and public-health teams can request reviewed access for research, preparedness, and resilience work under what OpenAI describes as clear public-benefit boundaries. A separate Rosalind Biodefense program supports trusted developers and public-health teams building defensive applications with GPT-Rosalind, with focus areas that include early detection, preparedness, diagnostics, response, and medical countermeasures. OpenAI said its broader vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines, and it described bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind as a step toward that vision. OpenAI describes the present moment as an inflection point at which AI can take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows.

Scientists and program leaders hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, which OpenAI says frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. Orchestra’s agents pinpoint the activities and timelines a problem touches, pull together the relevant information, and compare response options, and scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next.
