coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday.

Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call.
OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind.
Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other.
OpenAI says the combined team will build agents that connect scientific findings with the decisions and follow-up studies needed to turn a promising result into an actual medicine.
Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists.
In April, OpenAI launched GPT-Rosalind , a model built specifically for biology and drug discovery, and restricted it to vetted U.S. enterprise customers such as Amgen and Moderna.
In January alone, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health , which lets users connect their medical records to the chatbot, and bought records startup Torch for a reported $100 million to build it out.

Anthropic, OpenAI's closest rival, has been running the same play: it bought AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April and launched a research platform called Claude Science in June.
OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.

OpenAI announced the acquisition on October 20, 2026. OpenAI said its goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work required to turn those discoveries into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine takes roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery through regulatory approval in the United States, according to the company, and the teams behind those programs must coordinate work across internal departments and external partners, often through disconnected systems. OpenAI describes the present moment as an inflection point at which AI can take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind is OpenAI’s life sciences brand. OpenAI describes GPT-Rosalind as a purpose-built model that helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry, and Rosalind Workbench as the layer that connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data so researchers can analyze results and plan experiments. OpenAI said that together the organizations aim to build agents that connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio built its platform around a model in which people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders hand off the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, which OpenAI says frees them to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. According to OpenAI, a problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others: a failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents pinpoint the activities and timelines a problem touches, pull together the relevant information, and compare response options, and scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Orchestra Bio confirmed the acquisition on its own website, saying it started the company four years earlier to help biotech and pharma teams advance their drug development programs. The company describes medicine development as involving thousands of decisions and dependencies that run across discovery, preclinical, manufacturing, and clinical work. In its framing, agents can take on planning, orchestration, and analysis, leaving scientists and program leaders to concentrate on the decisions that require their expertise. Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters. Rosalind Workbench is in research preview, with an orchestrated set of scientific tools connected in a single workspace. It offers an Explore mode for general scientific questions, using the latest ChatGPT models available to the user, and a Research mode that applies GPT-Rosalind to more complex biological questions, in-depth analysis, and advanced research workflows, with access through an application process. Researchers can also use GPT-Rosalind inside Codex to connect their scientific tools, data, and evidence into research workflows that teams can review, share, and reuse, while a GPT-Rosalind API targets organizations that want to integrate life sciences reasoning into their own research applications, internal tools, and governed workflows. API access is subject to eligibility review and organizational approval. OpenAI’s product page reports benchmark results for the model on life sciences research tasks, stated as increases in performance per token: 53.7% on Genebench, 18.0% on Medchem Bench, 19.6% on Labworkbench, and 4.42% on LifeSci Bench. The page lists supported uses that include prioritizing biological targets, engineering proteins, synthesizing evidence across papers and experiments, analyzing unstructured experimental results, and saving workflows that teams can inspect, share, and reuse. OpenAI said its partnership with Novo Nordisk is aimed at translating the drugmaker’s scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance, and that at Moderna, AI is helping teams turn insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. In a statement carried on OpenAI’s Rosalind page , Mike Doustdar, Novo Nordisk’s CEO and president, said: “Our partnership with OpenAI will help translate this scale into faster R&D and commercial execution, while maintaining the governance our patients and society expect.” OpenAI also lists structured access routes beyond enterprise customers. The Rosalind Academic Plan offers eligible labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery. An enterprise option brings GPT-Rosalind into approved research workflows with governance review and enterprise-grade deployment controls, while government and public-health teams can request reviewed access for research, preparedness, and resilience work under what OpenAI describes as clear public-benefit boundaries. A separate Rosalind Biodefense program supports trusted developers and public-health teams building defensive applications with GPT-Rosalind, with focus areas that include early detection, preparedness, diagnostics, response, and medical countermeasures. OpenAI said its broader vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines, and it described bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind as a step toward that vision. story.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business

facts.text: OpenAI has bought Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco startup whose AI agents help drug companies keep sprawling development programs on schedule, the ChatGPT maker announced Tuesday.

Orchestra's AI agents—software that can watch over tasks and flag problems on its own—work out which activities and deadlines take the hit, gather the relevant information and compare ways to respond, while scientists and program leaders make the final call.
OpenAI did not say what it paid for Orchestra or when its agents will show up inside Rosalind.
Beyond the science itself, OpenAI says drug teams have to coordinate work across internal departments and outside partners, often relying on systems that don't talk to each other.
OpenAI says the combined team will build agents that connect scientific findings with the decisions and follow-up studies needed to turn a promising result into an actual medicine.
Orchestra's team and platform will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's family of AI models and tools for biologists and chemists.
In April, OpenAI launched GPT-Rosalind , a model built specifically for biology and drug discovery, and restricted it to vetted U.S. enterprise customers such as Amgen and Moderna.
In January alone, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health , which lets users connect their medical records to the chatbot, and bought records startup Torch for a reported $100 million to build it out.

Anthropic, OpenAI's closest rival, has been running the same play: it bought AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April and launched a research platform called Claude Science in June.
OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

Orchestra adds a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development.
Orchestra Bio said it is joining OpenAI “to continue our mission at an even greater scale,” and it thanked its customers, investors, and supporters.

To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie.
SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.
That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa.
Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla.

extraction.body: SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said he favored combining his two biggest companies. Finn Gomez / Getty Tech billionaire Elon Musk said Tuesday that the boards of SpaceX and Tesla had separately formed special committees to discuss the idea of a merger, taking a small step toward the possible consolidation of his two biggest companies. Musk, who is the CEO of both companies, said that the special committees had not reached an agreement and that there was no guarantee they would. He said a merger would require support from both sets of shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. Musk spoke about the potential tie-up during a call with Wall Street analysts about SpaceX’s quarterly results, which surpassed estimates; the company’s revenue more than doubled in part from renting out computing capacity to other artificial intelligence firms. In January, Tesla announced that it was investing about $2 billion to acquire shares in an AI startup that’s a subsidiary of SpaceX. Musk said that, because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations, he is not a member of either special committee or involved in the talks. He said the committees consist of the two boards’ independent directors but did not specify the memberships. “It’s an odd Kabuki dance, where groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” he said during the earnings calls. He also said that even answering a question about the idea from an analyst felt like “dancing through a minefield.” Musk, though, endorsed the idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies, as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” he said. Musk has already consolidated some of his other holdings. Last year, he merged his social media company, X, with his AI startup, called at the time xAI. Then, in February, SpaceX acquired xAI , which Musk has since renamed SpaceXSI.

SpaceX shares climbed about 8% in extended trading on Tuesday after the company reported 161% revenue growth for the third quarter, beating Wall Street estimates, with its artificial intelligence business growing ninefold. On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla , his automaker, would be a "good idea," adding that the boards of both companies have formed special committees to discuss a tie-up. Tesla reports third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday. Here's how SpaceX did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: Buzz has been building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation. SpaceX jumped into AI with the purchase earlier this year of xAI, Musk's AI lab. The company has been rapidly expanding that business by renting out capacity to Google , Anthropic and others. AI, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," has emerged as its largest business. Revenue jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Analysts expected sales of $6.47 billion, according to StreetAccount. During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor. SpaceX's launch business generated $1.77 billion in revenue in the third quarter. The company touted its Starship Flight 14 as a major milestone on the earnings call, and Musk said SpaceX will attempt to "catch both the booster and the ship," during its next test flight of the massive rocket. He added that SpaceX has a "steady stream of Starship flight attempts" scheduled through the end of this year, and accelerating next year. The company recently announced plans to build a $100 billion spaceport in Louisiana. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on the call that SpaceX aims to conduct its first launch from the facility by 2029. Musk said the first launch may be possible by the end of 2028. The U.S. Department of Justice lost its bid to have a federal court in Mississippi toss a lawsuit filed by the NAACP against SpaceX alleging Clean Air Act violations by Musk's company in the Memphis area. The DOJ had accused the NAACP of threatening "American national, economic, and energy security" by asking the court to temporarily shut off of the power supply used by SpaceX at its Colossus data centers. Musk said the boards at Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger "at the request of shareholders," noting that these groups "consist of independent directors." Because Musk is a "conflicted party," he said he can't be in the discussions. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said, referring to the development of software, chips and more. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." Musk said that on the Tesla side, "we will need a 50% vote of all shares -- not just those who vote -- but of all shareholders, and that's quite a high hurdle." Venture capitalist Ira Ehrenpreis is on the boards of both companies. Musk said on the call that SpaceX aims to reach "volume production" of AI chips, now in development with partners Tesla and Intel , during the third quarter of 2028 at the Terafab factory that's planned in Texas. Musk thanked ASML and other suppliers for prioritizing equipment deliveries for the factory. Musk previously pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and President Donald Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." The Journal, citing a person familiar with the situation, said Musk talked to senior administration officials, including Trump, "before imposing the new speed cap." The limits caused Ukraine's drones to lose Starshield connectivity when traveling at speed over 100 miles per hour. passages: The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger.
The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing .
It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.
Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent.
Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX.
Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.

extraction.body: This is CNBC's live coverage of SpaceX's 2026 third-quarter earnings. SpaceX shares climbed about 8% in extended trading on Tuesday after the company reported 161% revenue growth for the third quarter, beating Wall Street estimates, with its artificial intelligence business growing ninefold. On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla , his automaker, would be a "good idea," adding that the boards of both companies have formed special committees to discuss a tie-up. Tesla reports third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday. Here's how SpaceX did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: Buzz has been building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation. SpaceX jumped into AI with the purchase earlier this year of xAI, Musk's AI lab. The company has been rapidly expanding that business by renting out capacity to Google , Anthropic and others. AI, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," has emerged as its largest business. Revenue jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Analysts expected sales of $6.47 billion, according to StreetAccount. During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor. SpaceX's launch business generated $1.77 billion in revenue in the third quarter. The company touted its Starship Flight 14 as a major milestone on the earnings call, and Musk said SpaceX will attempt to "catch both the booster and the ship," during its next test flight of the massive rocket. He added that SpaceX has a "steady stream of Starship flight attempts" scheduled through the end of this year, and accelerating next year. The company recently announced plans to build a $100 billion spaceport in Louisiana. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on the call that SpaceX aims to conduct its first launch from the facility by 2029. Musk said the first launch may be possible by the end of 2028. The U.S. Department of Justice lost its bid to have a federal court in Mississippi toss a lawsuit filed by the NAACP against SpaceX alleging Clean Air Act violations by Musk's company in the Memphis area. The DOJ had accused the NAACP of threatening "American national, economic, and energy security" by asking the court to temporarily shut off of the power supply used by SpaceX at its Colossus data centers. Musk said the boards at Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger "at the request of shareholders," noting that these groups "consist of independent directors." Because Musk is a "conflicted party," he said he can't be in the discussions. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said, referring to the development of software, chips and more. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." Musk said that on the Tesla side, "we will need a 50% vote of all shares -- not just those who vote -- but of all shareholders, and that's quite a high hurdle." Venture capitalist Ira Ehrenpreis is on the boards of both companies. Musk said on the call that SpaceX aims to reach "volume production" of AI chips, now in development with partners Tesla and Intel , during the third quarter of 2028 at the Terafab factory that's planned in Texas. Musk thanked ASML and other suppliers for prioritizing equipment deliveries for the factory. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing .
It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.

Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX.

SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) plans to catch a returning Starship upper stage with its launch tower for the first time this month. "I'd say things look very good, and that's why we, assuming we receive regulatory approval to do so, will attempt to catch the Ship with the tower on the next flight, which is tentatively scheduled for the end of this month," CEO Elon Musk said on the company's Aug. 4 earnings call, its first since going public in June. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The confidence traces to Flight 13, which flew July 24 and ended with the Ship surviving reentry and splashing down softly in the Indian Ocean. Flight 14 is also slated to put Starlink V3 satellites into an operational orbit for the first time. Two steps sit between here and the attempt: the preflight engine firings both vehicles still have to complete, and the regulatory sign-off Musk named. The company's towers have caught the returning Super Heavy booster before, but never the Ship, which comes back from space at far higher speeds. The reason a catch matters is money. Starship's economics rest on both halves of the rocket flying again quickly -- a booster and Ship recovered at the tower are meant to be turned around and reflown instead of rebuilt. And a tower catch is the version of reuse that saves the most. The vehicle lands where it launched, gets inspected, and gets restacked, with no ocean recovery in between. For now, the finances run through Starlink. SpaceX's connectivity segment grew revenue 66% year over year to $4.3 billion last quarter, the only segment operating at a profit, while the company overall narrowed its net loss to $541 million from $1.0 billion on revenue that nearly doubled to $7.8 billion. The company also closed the quarter with $100 billion of cash and marketable securities and a $47.5 billion backlog, resources it says are going into Starship, Starlink satellites, and its artificial intelligence (AI) platform. The V3 satellites Flight 14 would carry are the larger generation that the network's next capacity step depends on. Of course, a tentative date is just that. The flight could slip into September, and the regulatory review isn't on the company's clock. A missed catch wouldn't end the program, either. Test flights exist to find the failures. But a catch that works would be the first time the Ship itself came back to the tower. extraction.body: SpaceX is planning to launch its next Starship test flight as soon as this month, CEO Elon Musk said on August 4 at the company's first earnings call. The mission will send the first upgraded Starlink satellites into orbit. It will also try to land the rocket's massive upper stage for the first time. This marks a big step up from the last test in July, when the upper stage showed better landing skills over the Indian Ocean. However, the plan still depends on getting regulatory approval, Musk said, adding that Starship's launch pace should "increase rapidly" in the coming months.Landing the upper stage, known as the "ship," is key to SpaceX's goal of building the world's first fully reusable orbital rocket system. Musk wants to use this system to grow the Starlink broadband network. NASA is also watching closely, since it plans to use Starship as a moon lander.SpaceX to seek regulatory approval for its next rocket launch dateSpaceX is currently pulling the 13th test's rocket stage out of the ocean for inspection, based on satellite images from Vantor. During the earnings call, Elon Musk said the exact launch date, and whether the ship will attempt a landing, depends on approval from regulators. "Assuming we receive regulatory approval to do so, we'll attempt to catch the ship with the tower on the next flight, which is tentatively scheduled for the end of this month," Musk said.The 14th Starship flight will carry the first batch of V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. Elon Musk said these satellites are "expected to deliver 10 times the amount of broadband capacity and data density from our current generations." SpaceX has said in its IPO prospectus that it eventually wants to launch 60 such satellites per Starship mission, across dozens of future flights.How the catch-and-land system worksA successful landing would mean catching the ship using giant mechanical arms on the launch tower in Texas. SpaceX has already used these arms to catch the rocket's Super Heavy booster three times, most recently in March 2025. Musk's long-term goal is for the tower to catch both parts. Super Heavy would be caught first, then quickly moved aside. About 90 minutes later, the ship would return after circling Earth and get caught too."Probably a year from now, we will be doing at least one flight a day, possibly more," Musk said at the earnings call.Get the latest technology news and updates.

Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages).

The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence").

SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) plans to catch a returning Starship upper stage with its launch tower for the first time this month. "I'd say things look very good, and that's why we, assuming we receive regulatory approval to do so, will attempt to catch the Ship with the tower on the next flight, which is tentatively scheduled for the end of this month," CEO Elon Musk said on the company's Aug. 4 earnings call, its first since going public in June. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The confidence traces to Flight 13, which flew July 24 and ended with the Ship surviving reentry and splashing down softly in the Indian Ocean. Flight 14 is also slated to put Starlink V3 satellites into an operational orbit for the first time. Two steps sit between here and the attempt: the preflight engine firings both vehicles still have to complete, and the regulatory sign-off Musk named. The company's towers have caught the returning Super Heavy booster before, but never the Ship, which comes back from space at far higher speeds. The reason a catch matters is money. Starship's economics rest on both halves of the rocket flying again quickly -- a booster and Ship recovered at the tower are meant to be turned around and reflown instead of rebuilt. And a tower catch is the version of reuse that saves the most. The vehicle lands where it launched, gets inspected, and gets restacked, with no ocean recovery in between. For now, the finances run through Starlink. SpaceX's connectivity segment grew revenue 66% year over year to $4.3 billion last quarter, the only segment operating at a profit, while the company overall narrowed its net loss to $541 million from $1.0 billion on revenue that nearly doubled to $7.8 billion. The company also closed the quarter with $100 billion of cash and marketable securities and a $47.5 billion backlog, resources it says are going into Starship, Starlink satellites, and its artificial intelligence (AI) platform. The V3 satellites Flight 14 would carry are the larger generation that the network's next capacity step depends on. Of course, a tentative date is just that. The flight could slip into September, and the regulatory review isn't on the company's clock. A missed catch wouldn't end the program, either. Test flights exist to find the failures. But a catch that works would be the first time the Ship itself came back to the tower. And with the stock around $141 as of this writing and the company valued near $1.9 trillion, the reusability case is arguably carrying a lot of that price. extraction.body: SpaceX is planning to launch its next Starship test flight as soon as this month, CEO Elon Musk said on August 4 at the company's first earnings call. The mission will send the first upgraded Starlink satellites into orbit. It will also try to land the rocket's massive upper stage for the first time. This marks a big step up from the last test in July, when the upper stage showed better landing skills over the Indian Ocean. However, the plan still depends on getting regulatory approval, Musk said, adding that Starship's launch pace should "increase rapidly" in the coming months.Landing the upper stage, known as the "ship," is key to SpaceX's goal of building the world's first fully reusable orbital rocket system. Musk wants to use this system to grow the Starlink broadband network. NASA is also watching closely, since it plans to use Starship as a moon lander.SpaceX to seek regulatory approval for its next rocket launch dateSpaceX is currently pulling the 13th test's rocket stage out of the ocean for inspection, based on satellite images from Vantor. During the earnings call, Elon Musk said the exact launch date, and whether the ship will attempt a landing, depends on approval from regulators. "Assuming we receive regulatory approval to do so, we'll attempt to catch the ship with the tower on the next flight, which is tentatively scheduled for the end of this month," Musk said.The 14th Starship flight will carry the first batch of V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. Elon Musk said these satellites are "expected to deliver 10 times the amount of broadband capacity and data density from our current generations." SpaceX has said in its IPO prospectus that it eventually wants to launch 60 such satellites per Starship mission, across dozens of future flights.How the catch-and-land system worksA successful landing would mean catching the ship using giant mechanical arms on the launch tower in Texas. SpaceX has already used these arms to catch the rocket's Super Heavy booster three times, most recently in March 2025. Musk's long-term goal is for the tower to catch both parts. Super Heavy would be caught first, then quickly moved aside. About 90 minutes later, the ship would return after circling Earth and get caught too."Probably a year from now, we will be doing at least one flight a day, possibly more," Musk said at the earnings call.Get the latest technology news and updates.

extraction.body: Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air. “I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste. “The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.” The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

“The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.”
The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

extraction.body: A 2025 doctoral study (opens in a new tab) by Lingyang Ding (opens in a new tab) , conducted in the Department of Chemical Engineering and Applied Chemistry at the University of Toronto under the supervision of Professor Gisele Azimi (opens in a new tab) , examines whether rare earth elements (REEs) can be extracted and separated from ion-adsorption clays using a more environmentally sustainable method than today’s dominant industrial practices. Drawing on laboratory experiments and process modeling, the research shows that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can selectively separate light and heavy rare earths from South American ion-adsorption clays—potentially offering a cleaner alternative to solvent extraction. However, the work also underscores a sobering reality: even promising new technologies face steep hurdles when set against China’s entrenched dominance in rare earth processing and separation. The dissertation investigates ion-adsorption clays, a class of rare-earth deposits best known from southern China but also found in parts of South America. Unlike hard-rock rare earth ores, these clays hold rare earth ions loosely on mineral surfaces, allowing extraction under milder chemical conditions. Ding first characterized the clay mineralogy and rare earth distribution, then developed a hydrometallurgical desorption process to release the elements into solution. The core innovation lies in the separation step, instead of conventional solvent extraction—which relies on large volumes of organic chemicals and generates significant waste—the study tests electrodialysis assisted by chelating agents (EDTA). By applying an electric field across selective membranes, the process encourages different rare earth ions to migrate at different rates, enabling separation of heavy rare earths (such as dysprosium) from light rare earths (such as neodymium and praseodymium). Laboratory experiments were paired with process simulations to evaluate energy use, purity, and scalability. The research demonstrates that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can achieve meaningful separation between heavy and light rare earths, with dysprosium selectively concentrated under optimized conditions. Compared with traditional solvent extraction, the method shows potential advantages in chemical intensity, environmental footprint, and process controllability. The work also advances scientific understanding of how rare earths bind to clay minerals and how they can be released efficiently. Crucially, the study confirms that ion-adsorption clays outside China could represent a viable supplemental source of high-value rare earths, particularly heavy rare earths that are critical for permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense systems. While technically promising, the findings also highlight a strategic constraint. China controls the overwhelming majority of global rare earth separation capacity, built over decades of industrial learning, capital investment, and regulatory tolerance. Even if cleaner separation technologies emerge in Western laboratories, translating them into commercial-scale processing plants requires infrastructure, skilled labor, permitting, and—most importantly—time. This study illustrates a broader lesson for policymakers and investors: innovation alone does not dismantle monopolies. Without parallel investment in scale-up, supply chain integration, and industrial policy, new extraction and separation technologies risk remaining confined to pilot plants while China continues to dominate downstream processing. The research is pre-commercial and laboratory-scale. Performance metrics such as energy consumption, membrane durability, throughput, and cost competitiveness at an industrial scale remain uncertain. The process also relies on chelating agents (such as EDTA), raising questions about reagent recovery, lifecycle impacts, and regulatory acceptance. Moreover, ion-adsorption clays vary significantly by geography. Results from a South American sample may not translate directly to other deposits without additional site-specific testing. The study does not claim to replace solvent extraction universally, but rather to offer a potential alternative under certain conditions. Ding’s work provides an important proof-of-concept for cleaner rare earth separation and reinforces the strategic value of non-Chinese ion-adsorption clay resources. At the same time, it serves as a reality check: breaking China’s rare earth processing monopoly will require not just better chemistry, but coordinated industrial execution. For ex-China supply chains to succeed, technological innovation must be matched by policy clarity, capital commitment, and long-term planning. Source: Ding, L. extraction.body: Rare-earth metals are critical to the high-tech society we live in as an essential component of mobile phones, computers and many other everyday devices. But increasing demand and limited global supply means we must urgently find a way to recover these metals efficiently from discarded products. Rare-earth metals are currently mined or recovered via traditional e-waste recycling. But there are drawbacks, including high cost, environmental damage, pollution and risks to human safety. This is where our ongoing research comes in. Our team in collaboration with the research centre Tecnalia in Spain has developed a way to use environmentally friendly chemicals to recover rare-earth metals. It involves a process called “electrodeposition”, in which a low electric current causes the metals to deposit on a desired surface. This is important because if we roll out our process to scale, we can alleviate the pressure on global supply, and reduce our reliance on mining. Rare-earth metals is the collective name for a group of 17 elements: 15 from the “lanthanides series” in the periodic table, along with the elements scandium and yttrium. These elements have unique catalytic, metallurgical, nuclear, electrical, magnetic and luminescent properties. The term “rare” refers to their even, but scarce, distribution around the world, noted after they were first discovered in the late 18th century. These minerals are critical components of electronic devices, and vital for many green technologies; they’re in magnets for wind power turbines and in batteries for hybrid-electric vehicles. In fact, up to 600 kilograms of rare-earth metals are required to operate just one wind turbine. The annual demand for rare-earth metals doubled to 125,000 tonnes in 15 years, and the demand is projected to reach 315,000 tonnes in 2030, driven by increasing uptake in green technologies and advancing electronics. This is creating enormous pressure on global production. Rare-earth metals are currently extracted through mining, which comes with a number of downsides. First, it’s costly and inefficient because extracting even a very small amount of rare earth metals requires large areas to be mined. Second, the process can have enormous environmental impacts. Mining for rare earth minerals generates large volumes of toxic and radioactive material, due to the co-extraction of thorium and uranium — radioactive metals which can cause problems for the environment and human health. Third, most mining for rare-earth metals occurs in China, which produces more than 70% of global supply. This raises concerns about long-term availability, particularly after China threatened to restrict its supply in 2019 during its trade war with the US. Through e-waste recycling, rare-earth metals can be recovered from electronic products such as mobile phones, laptops and electric vehicles batteries, once they reach the end of their life. For example, recovering them from electric vehicle batteries involves traditional hydrometallurgical (corrosive media treatment) and pyrometallurgical (heat treatment) processes. But these have several drawbacks. Similar recovery processes are also applied to other energy storage technologies, such as lithium ion batteries. Given these challenges, we set out to find a sustainable method to recover rare-earth metals, using electrodeposition. Electrodeposition is already used to recover other metals. In our case, we have designed an environmentally friendly composition based on ionic liquid (salt-based) systems . We focused on recovering neodymium, an important rare-earth metal due to its outstanding magnetic properties, and in extremely high demand compared to other rare-earth metals. It’s used in electric motors in cars, mobile phones, wind turbines, hard disk drives and audio devices. Ionic liquids are highly stable, which means it’s possible to recover neodymium without generating side products, which can affect the neodymium purity. The novelty of our research using ionic liquids for electrodeposition is the presence of water in the mix, which improves the quantity of the final recovered neodymium metal. Unlike previously reported methods, we can recover neodymium metal without using controlled atmosphere, and at working temperature lower than 100°C. These are key considerations to industrialising such a technology. At this stage we have proof of concept at lab scale using a solution of ionic liquid with water, recovering neodymium in its most expensive metallic form in a few hours. We are currently looking at scaling up the process. In time, our method could avoid the need to mine for rare earth metals and minimises the generation of toxic and harmful waste. It also promises to help increase economic returns from e-waste. Importantly, this method could be adapted to recover metals in other end-of-life applications, such as lithium ion batteries, as a 2019 report projected an 11% growth per annum in production in Europe. Our research is an important early step towards establishing a clean and sustainable processing route for rare-earth metals, and alleviating the pressures on these critical elements. extraction.body: Rare earth elements such as lanthanum, neodymium and dysprosium are used to build the electric motor in your car, the LED lights in your house and the MRI machine at your doctor’s office. But first, they have to be mined and separated from each other. Historically, that purification has been a costly, difficult process, relying on huge amounts of toxic chemicals. Now, researchers in the lab of Assoc. Prof. Chong Liu at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), working with colleagues at Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory, have discovered a cleaner method to separate rare earth elements from each other. The new approach relies on a layered form of manganese oxide—a mineral material with the right size layers to allow ions to slip in and out and to differentiate rare earth elements. “This is the first time that people have used electrochemical intercalation and harnessed the structural characteristics to separate similar lanthanides, which are intrinsically very hard to separate,” said Liu, senior author of the new study, which published in Nature Chemical Engineering . “What’s also valuable is that we provided a lot of new understanding of how rare earth ions are interacting with this material and how we can manipulate it to better selectivity.” “This kind of separation is competitive with other rare earth separation methods, but it’s done in water, without organic solvents,” said George Schatz, professor of chemistry at Northwestern and a co-author of the study. “That’s a difference that could actually matter at manufacturing scale.” The 17 rare earth elements—including the 15 lanthanides, plus scandium and yttrium—rarely occur alone. They’re almost always mined together and chemically they’re nearly identical, with only tiny differences in ion size and acidity differentiating each one. Pulling them apart typically requires custom-built molecules and large amounts of acid, which is used to strip each element off those molecules. “Rare earths always come mixed together, whether they’re in an ore or in a waste stream, and separating them from each other is a second, very challenging step even after you’ve pulled them away from everything else,” said UChicago PME graduate student Jiadong Liu, a co-first author of the new paper. Chong Liu and her colleagues knew that one of the differences between rare earth ions was the size of the water shell surrounding each one when they are dissolved in solution. Lighter rare earths like lanthanum have a larger first water shell, while heavier rare earths like dysprosium have a smaller first shell. Taking advantage of that size difference, Chong Liu’s group engineered manganese oxide so that the gaps between its stacked layers were only a few water molecules wide. Then, they squeezed raw mixtures of rare earth elements inside. The approach divided the elements into two groups. Heavier lanthanides with smaller water shells stuck in the channels more tightly. Lighter lanthanides with larger shells pushed the layers apart, loosening their grip. passages: Rare earth elements such as lanthanum, neodymium and dysprosium are used to build the electric motor in your car, the LED lights in your house and the MRI machine at your doctor’s office.
But first, they have to be mined and separated from each other. Historically, that purification has been a costly, difficult process, relying on huge amounts of toxic chemicals.

Now, researchers in the lab of Assoc. Prof. Chong Liu at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), working with colleagues at Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory, have discovered a cleaner method to separate rare earth elements from each other.
The new approach relies on a layered form of manganese oxide—a mineral material with the right size layers to allow ions to slip in and out and to differentiate rare earth elements.

“This is the first time that people have used electrochemical intercalation and harnessed the structural characteristics to separate similar lanthanides, which are intrinsically very hard to separate,” said Liu, senior author of the new study, which published in Nature Chemical Engineering . “What’s also valuable is that we provided a lot of new understanding of how rare earth ions are interacting with this material and how we can manipulate it to better selectivity.”

“This kind of separation is competitive with other rare earth separation methods, but it’s done in water, without organic solvents,” said George Schatz, professor of chemistry at Northwestern and a co-author of the study. “That’s a difference that could actually matter at manufacturing scale.”

The 17 rare earth elements—including the 15 lanthanides, plus scandium and yttrium—rarely occur alone. They’re almost always mined together and chemically they’re nearly identical, with only tiny differences in ion size and acidity differentiating each one. Pulling them apart typically requires custom-built molecules and large amounts of acid, which is used to strip each element off those molecules.

“Rare earths always come mixed together, whether they’re in an ore or in a waste stream, and separating them from each other is a second, very challenging step even after you’ve pulled them away from everything else,” said UChicago PME graduate student Jiadong Liu, a co-first author of the new paper.

Chong Liu and her colleagues knew that one of the differences between rare earth ions was the size of the water shell surrounding each one when they are dissolved in solution. Lighter rare earths like lanthanum have a larger first water shell, while heavier rare earths like dysprosium have a smaller first shell.

Taking advantage of that size difference, Chong Liu’s group engineered manganese oxide so that the gaps between its stacked layers were only a few water molecules wide. Then, they squeezed raw mixtures of rare earth elements inside.

The approach divided the elements into two groups. Heavier lanthanides with smaller water shells stuck in the channels more tightly. Lighter lanthanides with larger shells pushed the layers apart, loosening their grip.

To confirm what was happening at a molecular level, the UChicago PME team collaborated with Schatz’s group at Northwestern to run quantum mechanical simulations using a method called density functional theory, which predicts how atoms arrange themselves and interact based on the underlying physics. They also worked with Argonne scientists to obtain experimental X-ray data.

“It was incredibly rewarding to see how closely our density functional theory calculations matched the synchrotron X-ray measurements,” said co-first author Woo Cheol Jeon, who conducted the research as a postdoctoral researcher in Schatz’s lab at Northwestern. “The calculations let us see, atom by atom, how each rare earth element arranges its hydration shell inside the confined channel, which experiments couldn’t resolve directly.”

While the new process separated the heaviest and lightest rare earths, some of the most useful elements still behaved too similarly to separate. To fine-tune the purification so that it could differentiate similar pairs of rare earth elements, the research team used an electric current and added magnesium ions.

The magnesium acted as a scaffold, holding the manganese oxide channels to their designed spacing, even when rare earth elements tried to expand it—an effect called pinning. Now, rare earth ions showed differences in binding to the layered material even when they were extremely similar.

“Even elements that behave almost identically will still try to expand the material to make room for their water molecules,” said Siqi Zou, PhD'24, co-first author of the study and former UChicago PME graduate student. “By pinning the channel so it can’t expand at all, we forced that small difference in behavior to become a much bigger difference in how strongly each element binds.”

With the addition of magnesium, the enrichment of neodymium over lanthanum jumped from a 1.6-fold difference to a 5.4-fold difference. After two cycles of purification, researchers could get a neodymium sample that was 97% pure. Similar improvements were seen for other rare earth elements.
The new purification method could ultimately point toward different ways of thinking about where rare earth processing happens, the researchers said.

“Right now, rare earth ores get mined all over the world, but almost all of them end up being sent overseas for processing,” said Schatz, co-author of the study. “A method like this, that just uses water and electricity instead of organic solvents, is the kind of technology that could actually change how and where that processing gets done.”

The method isn’t yet ready to be scaled up to replace industrial purification. Still, it points to a broader design principle: tuning a channel’s width can determine which ions a material prefers, even for ions that differ by a fraction of an angstrom.

Chong Liu’s group is now testing the approach against more of the 15 lanthanides, while Schatz is refining his computational models, aiming to explain the pinning effect more quantitatively. He is also using the same modeling approach developed for this work to study other materials.

coreStoryFacts.text: In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste.
The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

Drawing on laboratory experiments and process modeling, the research shows that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can selectively separate light and heavy rare earths from South American ion-adsorption clays—potentially offering a cleaner alternative to solvent extraction.
However, the work also underscores a sobering reality: even promising new technologies face steep hurdles when set against China’s entrenched dominance in rare earth processing and separation.
While technically promising, the findings also highlight a strategic constraint.
China controls the overwhelming majority of global rare earth separation capacity, built over decades of industrial learning, capital investment, and regulatory tolerance.

Even if cleaner separation technologies emerge in Western laboratories, translating them into commercial-scale processing plants requires infrastructure, skilled labor, permitting, and—most importantly—time.
For ex-China supply chains to succeed, technological innovation must be matched by policy clarity, capital commitment, and long-term planning.

A 2025 doctoral study (opens in a new tab) by Lingyang Ding (opens in a new tab) , conducted in the Department of Chemical Engineering and Applied Chemistry at the University of Toronto under the supervision of Professor Gisele Azimi (opens in a new tab) , examines whether rare earth elements (REEs) can be extracted and separated from ion-adsorption clays using a more environmentally sustainable method than today’s dominant industrial practices.
Unlike hard-rock rare earth ores, these clays hold rare earth ions loosely on mineral surfaces, allowing extraction under milder chemical conditions.
Ding first characterized the clay mineralogy and rare earth distribution, then developed a hydrometallurgical desorption process to release the elements into solution.
This study illustrates a broader lesson for policymakers and investors: innovation alone does not dismantle monopolies.

Without parallel investment in scale-up, supply chain integration, and industrial policy, new extraction and separation technologies risk remaining confined to pilot plants while China continues to dominate downstream processing.
© 2025 Rare Earth Exchanges™ – Accelerating Transparency, Accuracy, and Insight Across the Rare Earth & Critical Minerals Supply Chain.

The core innovation lies in the separation step, instead of conventional solvent extraction—which relies on large volumes of organic chemicals and generates significant waste—the study tests electrodialysis assisted by chelating agents (EDTA).
Rare-earth metals are critical to the high-tech society we live in as an essential component of mobile phones, computers and many other everyday devices.
But increasing demand and limited global supply means we must urgently find a way to recover these metals efficiently from discarded products.

Importantly, this method could be adapted to recover metals in other end-of-life applications, such as lithium ion batteries, as a 2019 report projected an 11% growth per annum in production in Europe.
For example, recovering them from electric vehicle batteries involves traditional hydrometallurgical (corrosive media treatment) and pyrometallurgical (heat treatment) processes.
Electrodeposition is already used to recover other metals.
Unlike previously reported methods, we can recover neodymium metal without using controlled atmosphere, and at working temperature lower than 100°C.
The novelty of our research using ionic liquids for electrodeposition is the presence of water in the mix, which improves the quantity of the final recovered neodymium metal.

extraction.body: Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air. “I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste. “The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.” The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

Drawing on laboratory experiments and process modeling, the research shows that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can selectively separate light and heavy rare earths from South American ion-adsorption clays—potentially offering a cleaner alternative to solvent extraction. However, the work also underscores a sobering reality: even promising new technologies face steep hurdles when set against China’s entrenched dominance in rare earth processing and separation. The dissertation investigates ion-adsorption clays, a class of rare-earth deposits best known from southern China but also found in parts of South America. Unlike hard-rock rare earth ores, these clays hold rare earth ions loosely on mineral surfaces, allowing extraction under milder chemical conditions. Ding first characterized the clay mineralogy and rare earth distribution, then developed a hydrometallurgical desorption process to release the elements into solution. The core innovation lies in the separation step, instead of conventional solvent extraction—which relies on large volumes of organic chemicals and generates significant waste—the study tests electrodialysis assisted by chelating agents (EDTA). By applying an electric field across selective membranes, the process encourages different rare earth ions to migrate at different rates, enabling separation of heavy rare earths (such as dysprosium) from light rare earths (such as neodymium and praseodymium). Laboratory experiments were paired with process simulations to evaluate energy use, purity, and scalability. The research demonstrates that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can achieve meaningful separation between heavy and light rare earths, with dysprosium selectively concentrated under optimized conditions. Compared with traditional solvent extraction, the method shows potential advantages in chemical intensity, environmental footprint, and process controllability. The work also advances scientific understanding of how rare earths bind to clay minerals and how they can be released efficiently. Crucially, the study confirms that ion-adsorption clays outside China could represent a viable supplemental source of high-value rare earths, particularly heavy rare earths that are critical for permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense systems. While technically promising, the findings also highlight a strategic constraint. China controls the overwhelming majority of global rare earth separation capacity, built over decades of industrial learning, capital investment, and regulatory tolerance. Even if cleaner separation technologies emerge in Western laboratories, translating them into commercial-scale processing plants requires infrastructure, skilled labor, permitting, and—most importantly—time. This study illustrates a broader lesson for policymakers and investors: innovation alone does not dismantle monopolies. Without parallel investment in scale-up, supply chain integration, and industrial policy, new extraction and separation technologies risk remaining confined to pilot plants while China continues to dominate downstream processing. The research is pre-commercial and laboratory-scale. Performance metrics such as energy consumption, membrane durability, throughput, and cost competitiveness at an industrial scale remain uncertain. The process also relies on chelating agents (such as EDTA), raising questions about reagent recovery, lifecycle impacts, and regulatory acceptance. Moreover, ion-adsorption clays vary significantly by geography. Results from a South American sample may not translate directly to other deposits without additional site-specific testing. The study does not claim to replace solvent extraction universally, but rather to offer a potential alternative under certain conditions. Ding’s work provides an important proof-of-concept for cleaner rare earth separation and reinforces the strategic value of non-Chinese ion-adsorption clay resources. extraction.body: Rare-earth metals are critical to the high-tech society we live in as an essential component of mobile phones, computers and many other everyday devices. But increasing demand and limited global supply means we must urgently find a way to recover these metals efficiently from discarded products. Rare-earth metals are currently mined or recovered via traditional e-waste recycling. But there are drawbacks, including high cost, environmental damage, pollution and risks to human safety. This is where our ongoing research comes in. Our team in collaboration with the research centre Tecnalia in Spain has developed a way to use environmentally friendly chemicals to recover rare-earth metals. It involves a process called “electrodeposition”, in which a low electric current causes the metals to deposit on a desired surface. This is important because if we roll out our process to scale, we can alleviate the pressure on global supply, and reduce our reliance on mining. Rare-earth metals is the collective name for a group of 17 elements: 15 from the “lanthanides series” in the periodic table, along with the elements scandium and yttrium. These elements have unique catalytic, metallurgical, nuclear, electrical, magnetic and luminescent properties. The term “rare” refers to their even, but scarce, distribution around the world, noted after they were first discovered in the late 18th century. These minerals are critical components of electronic devices, and vital for many green technologies; they’re in magnets for wind power turbines and in batteries for hybrid-electric vehicles. In fact, up to 600 kilograms of rare-earth metals are required to operate just one wind turbine. The annual demand for rare-earth metals doubled to 125,000 tonnes in 15 years, and the demand is projected to reach 315,000 tonnes in 2030, driven by increasing uptake in green technologies and advancing electronics. This is creating enormous pressure on global production. Rare-earth metals are currently extracted through mining, which comes with a number of downsides. First, it’s costly and inefficient because extracting even a very small amount of rare earth metals requires large areas to be mined. Second, the process can have enormous environmental impacts. Mining for rare earth minerals generates large volumes of toxic and radioactive material, due to the co-extraction of thorium and uranium — radioactive metals which can cause problems for the environment and human health. Third, most mining for rare-earth metals occurs in China, which produces more than 70% of global supply. This raises concerns about long-term availability, particularly after China threatened to restrict its supply in 2019 during its trade war with the US. Through e-waste recycling, rare-earth metals can be recovered from electronic products such as mobile phones, laptops and electric vehicles batteries, once they reach the end of their life. For example, recovering them from electric vehicle batteries involves traditional hydrometallurgical (corrosive media treatment) and pyrometallurgical (heat treatment) processes. But these have several drawbacks. Similar recovery processes are also applied to other energy storage technologies, such as lithium ion batteries. Given these challenges, we set out to find a sustainable method to recover rare-earth metals, using electrodeposition. Electrodeposition is already used to recover other metals. In our case, we have designed an environmentally friendly composition based on ionic liquid (salt-based) systems . We focused on recovering neodymium, an important rare-earth metal due to its outstanding magnetic properties, and in extremely high demand compared to other rare-earth metals. It’s used in electric motors in cars, mobile phones, wind turbines, hard disk drives and audio devices. Ionic liquids are highly stable, which means it’s possible to recover neodymium without generating side products, which can affect the neodymium purity. The novelty of our research using ionic liquids for electrodeposition is the presence of water in the mix, which improves the quantity of the final recovered neodymium metal. Unlike previously reported methods, we can recover neodymium metal without using controlled atmosphere, and at working temperature lower than 100°C. These are key considerations to industrialising such a technology. At this stage we have proof of concept at lab scale using a solution of ionic liquid with water, recovering neodymium in its most expensive metallic form in a few hours. We are currently looking at scaling up the process. In time, our method could avoid the need to mine for rare earth metals and minimises the generation of toxic and harmful waste. It also promises to help increase economic returns from e-waste. Importantly, this method could be adapted to recover metals in other end-of-life applications, such as lithium ion batteries, as a 2019 report projected an 11% growth per annum in production in Europe. Our research is an important early step towards establishing a clean and sustainable processing route for rare-earth metals, and alleviating the pressures on these critical elements. extraction.body: Rare earth elements such as lanthanum, neodymium and dysprosium are used to build the electric motor in your car, the LED lights in your house and the MRI machine at your doctor’s office. But first, they have to be mined and separated from each other. Historically, that purification has been a costly, difficult process, relying on huge amounts of toxic chemicals. Now, researchers in the lab of Assoc. Prof. Chong Liu at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), working with colleagues at Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory, have discovered a cleaner method to separate rare earth elements from each other. The new approach relies on a layered form of manganese oxide—a mineral material with the right size layers to allow ions to slip in and out and to differentiate rare earth elements. “This is the first time that people have used electrochemical intercalation and harnessed the structural characteristics to separate similar lanthanides, which are intrinsically very hard to separate,” said Liu, senior author of the new study, which published in Nature Chemical Engineering . “What’s also valuable is that we provided a lot of new understanding of how rare earth ions are interacting with this material and how we can manipulate it to better selectivity.” “This kind of separation is competitive with other rare earth separation methods, but it’s done in water, without organic solvents,” said George Schatz, professor of chemistry at Northwestern and a co-author of the study. “That’s a difference that could actually matter at manufacturing scale.” The 17 rare earth elements—including the 15 lanthanides, plus scandium and yttrium—rarely occur alone. They’re almost always mined together and chemically they’re nearly identical, with only tiny differences in ion size and acidity differentiating each one. Pulling them apart typically requires custom-built molecules and large amounts of acid, which is used to strip each element off those molecules. “Rare earths always come mixed together, whether they’re in an ore or in a waste stream, and separating them from each other is a second, very challenging step even after you’ve pulled them away from everything else,” said UChicago PME graduate student Jiadong Liu, a co-first author of the new paper. Chong Liu and her colleagues knew that one of the differences between rare earth ions was the size of the water shell surrounding each one when they are dissolved in solution. Lighter rare earths like lanthanum have a larger first water shell, while heavier rare earths like dysprosium have a smaller first shell. Taking advantage of that size difference, Chong Liu’s group engineered manganese oxide so that the gaps between its stacked layers were only a few water molecules wide. Then, they squeezed raw mixtures of rare earth elements inside. The approach divided the elements into two groups. Heavier lanthanides with smaller water shells stuck in the channels more tightly. Lighter lanthanides with larger shells pushed the layers apart, loosening their grip. To confirm what was happening at a molecular level, the UChicago PME team collaborated with Schatz’s group at Northwestern to run quantum mechanical simulations using a method called density functional theory, which predicts how atoms arrange themselves and interact based on the underlying physics. They also worked with Argonne scientists to obtain experimental X-ray data. “It was incredibly rewarding to see how closely our density functional theory calculations matched the synchrotron X-ray measurements,” said co-first author Woo Cheol Jeon, who conducted the research as a postdoctoral researcher in Schatz’s lab at Northwestern. “The calculations let us see, atom by atom, how each rare earth element arranges its hydration shell inside the confined channel, which experiments couldn’t resolve directly.” While the new process separated the heaviest and lightest rare earths, some of the most useful elements still behaved too similarly to separate. To fine-tune the purification so that it could differentiate similar pairs of rare earth elements, the research team used an electric current and added magnesium ions. The magnesium acted as a scaffold, holding the manganese oxide channels to their designed spacing, even when rare earth elements tried to expand it—an effect called pinning. Now, rare earth ions showed differences in binding to the layered material even when they were extremely similar. “Even elements that behave almost identically will still try to expand the material to make room for their water molecules,” said Siqi Zou, PhD'24, co-first author of the study and former UChicago PME graduate student. “By pinning the channel so it can’t expand at all, we forced that small difference in behavior to become a much bigger difference in how strongly each element binds.” With the addition of magnesium, the enrichment of neodymium over lanthanum jumped from a 1.6-fold difference to a 5.4-fold difference. After two cycles of purification, researchers could get a neodymium sample that was 97% pure. Similar improvements were seen for other rare earth elements.
