passages: Rare earth elements such as lanthanum, neodymium and dysprosium are used to build the electric motor in your car, the LED lights in your house and the MRI machine at your doctor’s office.
But first, they have to be mined and separated from each other. Historically, that purification has been a costly, difficult process, relying on huge amounts of toxic chemicals.

Now, researchers in the lab of Assoc. Prof. Chong Liu at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), working with colleagues at Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory, have discovered a cleaner method to separate rare earth elements from each other.
The new approach relies on a layered form of manganese oxide—a mineral material with the right size layers to allow ions to slip in and out and to differentiate rare earth elements.

“This is the first time that people have used electrochemical intercalation and harnessed the structural characteristics to separate similar lanthanides, which are intrinsically very hard to separate,” said Liu, senior author of the new study, which published in Nature Chemical Engineering . “What’s also valuable is that we provided a lot of new understanding of how rare earth ions are interacting with this material and how we can manipulate it to better selectivity.”

“This kind of separation is competitive with other rare earth separation methods, but it’s done in water, without organic solvents,” said George Schatz, professor of chemistry at Northwestern and a co-author of the study. “That’s a difference that could actually matter at manufacturing scale.”

The 17 rare earth elements—including the 15 lanthanides, plus scandium and yttrium—rarely occur alone. They’re almost always mined together and chemically they’re nearly identical, with only tiny differences in ion size and acidity differentiating each one. Pulling them apart typically requires custom-built molecules and large amounts of acid, which is used to strip each element off those molecules.

“Rare earths always come mixed together, whether they’re in an ore or in a waste stream, and separating them from each other is a second, very challenging step even after you’ve pulled them away from everything else,” said UChicago PME graduate student Jiadong Liu, a co-first author of the new paper.

Chong Liu and her colleagues knew that one of the differences between rare earth ions was the size of the water shell surrounding each one when they are dissolved in solution. Lighter rare earths like lanthanum have a larger first water shell, while heavier rare earths like dysprosium have a smaller first shell.

Taking advantage of that size difference, Chong Liu’s group engineered manganese oxide so that the gaps between its stacked layers were only a few water molecules wide. Then, they squeezed raw mixtures of rare earth elements inside.

The approach divided the elements into two groups. Heavier lanthanides with smaller water shells stuck in the channels more tightly. Lighter lanthanides with larger shells pushed the layers apart, loosening their grip.

To confirm what was happening at a molecular level, the UChicago PME team collaborated with Schatz’s group at Northwestern to run quantum mechanical simulations using a method called density functional theory, which predicts how atoms arrange themselves and interact based on the underlying physics. They also worked with Argonne scientists to obtain experimental X-ray data.

“It was incredibly rewarding to see how closely our density functional theory calculations matched the synchrotron X-ray measurements,” said co-first author Woo Cheol Jeon, who conducted the research as a postdoctoral researcher in Schatz’s lab at Northwestern. “The calculations let us see, atom by atom, how each rare earth element arranges its hydration shell inside the confined channel, which experiments couldn’t resolve directly.”

While the new process separated the heaviest and lightest rare earths, some of the most useful elements still behaved too similarly to separate. To fine-tune the purification so that it could differentiate similar pairs of rare earth elements, the research team used an electric current and added magnesium ions.

The magnesium acted as a scaffold, holding the manganese oxide channels to their designed spacing, even when rare earth elements tried to expand it—an effect called pinning. Now, rare earth ions showed differences in binding to the layered material even when they were extremely similar.

“Even elements that behave almost identically will still try to expand the material to make room for their water molecules,” said Siqi Zou, PhD'24, co-first author of the study and former UChicago PME graduate student. “By pinning the channel so it can’t expand at all, we forced that small difference in behavior to become a much bigger difference in how strongly each element binds.”

With the addition of magnesium, the enrichment of neodymium over lanthanum jumped from a 1.6-fold difference to a 5.4-fold difference. After two cycles of purification, researchers could get a neodymium sample that was 97% pure. Similar improvements were seen for other rare earth elements.
The new purification method could ultimately point toward different ways of thinking about where rare earth processing happens, the researchers said.

“Right now, rare earth ores get mined all over the world, but almost all of them end up being sent overseas for processing,” said Schatz, co-author of the study. “A method like this, that just uses water and electricity instead of organic solvents, is the kind of technology that could actually change how and where that processing gets done.”

The method isn’t yet ready to be scaled up to replace industrial purification. Still, it points to a broader design principle: tuning a channel’s width can determine which ions a material prefers, even for ions that differ by a fraction of an angstrom.

Chong Liu’s group is now testing the approach against more of the 15 lanthanides, while Schatz is refining his computational models, aiming to explain the pinning effect more quantitatively. He is also using the same modeling approach developed for this work to study other materials.

story.title: A cleaner path to rare earth metals

facts.text: In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste.
The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

Drawing on laboratory experiments and process modeling, the research shows that chelation-assisted electrodialysis can selectively separate light and heavy rare earths from South American ion-adsorption clays—potentially offering a cleaner alternative to solvent extraction.
However, the work also underscores a sobering reality: even promising new technologies face steep hurdles when set against China’s entrenched dominance in rare earth processing and separation.
While technically promising, the findings also highlight a strategic constraint.
China controls the overwhelming majority of global rare earth separation capacity, built over decades of industrial learning, capital investment, and regulatory tolerance.

Even if cleaner separation technologies emerge in Western laboratories, translating them into commercial-scale processing plants requires infrastructure, skilled labor, permitting, and—most importantly—time.
For ex-China supply chains to succeed, technological innovation must be matched by policy clarity, capital commitment, and long-term planning.
Unlike hard-rock rare earth ores, these clays hold rare earth ions loosely on mineral surfaces, allowing extraction under milder chemical conditions.
Ding first characterized the clay mineralogy and rare earth distribution, then developed a hydrometallurgical desorption process to release the elements into solution.
This study illustrates a broader lesson for policymakers and investors: innovation alone does not dismantle monopolies.

Without parallel investment in scale-up, supply chain integration, and industrial policy, new extraction and separation technologies risk remaining confined to pilot plants while China continues to dominate downstream processing.

The core innovation lies in the separation step, instead of conventional solvent extraction—which relies on large volumes of organic chemicals and generates significant waste—the study tests electrodialysis assisted by chelating agents (EDTA).
Rare-earth metals are critical to the high-tech society we live in as an essential component of mobile phones, computers and many other everyday devices.
But increasing demand and limited global supply means we must urgently find a way to recover these metals efficiently from discarded products.

Importantly, this method could be adapted to recover metals in other end-of-life applications, such as lithium ion batteries, as a 2019 report projected an 11% growth per annum in production in Europe.
For example, recovering them from electric vehicle batteries involves traditional hydrometallurgical (corrosive media treatment) and pyrometallurgical (heat treatment) processes.
Electrodeposition is already used to recover other metals.
Unlike previously reported methods, we can recover neodymium metal without using controlled atmosphere, and at working temperature lower than 100°C.
The novelty of our research using ionic liquids for electrodeposition is the presence of water in the mix, which improves the quantity of the final recovered neodymium metal.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.

Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:
“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”
In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said:

We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.

Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way.

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.

“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”

Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.

Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.

Security firm Claroc published those findings on October 18, exposing a structural problem with how Muse handled its link-sharing feature: "anyone with the link" turned out to mean considerably more people than you probably intended. Muse is Meta's general-purpose AI agent , capable of searching the web, filling out forms, booking appointments, and connecting to your accounts. That scope matters here, because this is not a note-taking app; it is a system with access to your calendar, professional correspondence, and connected services. Many services use opaque identifiers in share links, but Muse reportedly placed descriptive conversation titles inside the hostname itself, where network infrastructure could record them. According to Claroc's research, Muse's sharing feature placed the conversation title directly inside the subdomain of the sharing address, producing hostnames like q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information.
For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving.

Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively.

Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran.

extraction.body: Many early adopters of Instinct and Meta's Muse have said the digital assistants saved them time and money by searching the web, managing inboxes and calendars, disputing bills, booking travel, and making purchases. For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. The researchers did not report guessing a random string or exploiting a vulnerability in Muse's private sessions. Claroc reportedly searched records associated with Meta's content-delivery domain, retrieved the descriptive hostnames, and opened the pages from there.
Meta paused the sharing feature after Claroc reported the issue, but the episode raises broader questions about how AI agents handle each individual data path.

Meta told Ars Technica that Muse sharing creates pages accessible to people who have the link, and that it paused the feature while reviewing the report and considering changes to how the links can be discovered. Claroc had reported the findings through Meta's bug-bounty program on October 8, ten days before publishing its research publicly.

This is not evidence that every private Muse conversation leaked. The risk applied specifically to conversations users had deliberately shared through the feature, while unintended discoverability was the reported problem. Private sessions operated separately, according to Meta's documentation describing isolated cloud environments .

Muse is built to sit across your entire digital life, and that reach creates multiple data paths: private sessions, sharing features, connected-account integrations, and more. Think of it like a smart thermostat that also controls your front-door camera. The device itself may be secure, but each integration deserves its own scrutiny.

Treat any AI share link as potentially discoverable by secretly tracking users and infrastructure outside your control. Delete shared pages when the conversation has served its purpose, where deletion controls are available, and evaluate each sharing or integration feature on its own terms to stay safe . Your assistant's general privacy posture does not automatically extend to every button you click inside it.

Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

story.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations

facts.text: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday.
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions.
As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people.
The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
“What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.
People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link.

One passive-DNS query surfaced roughly 6,800 shared Meta Muse conversation links, some containing confidential files exposed to unintended audiences, including business notes, loan applications, and partial bank-account details.
This is not evidence that every private Muse conversation leaked.
The risk applied specifically to conversations users had deliberately shared through the feature, while unintended discoverability was the reported problem.
Private sessions operated separately, according to Meta's documentation describing isolated cloud environments .
Muse is built to sit across your entire digital life, and that reach creates multiple data paths: private sessions, sharing features, connected-account integrations, and more.
Muse is Meta's general-purpose AI agent , capable of searching the web, filling out forms, booking appointments, and connecting to your accounts.

sources.title: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act
passages: Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.
TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court.
The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR .
The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”
Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.
PT: The article was updated to include a statement from TikTok.

sources.title: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act - NPR
passages: TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company initially declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.
It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

After publication, TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown sent a statement saying the citations and claims in the story are "clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works."

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.

Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.)
They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony.
Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.
TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives. Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time. In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough." Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the court filings. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption "Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague. In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings. The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules. Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K. "If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut." Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law. Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering. If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena. In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions. TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices. The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content. The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit. Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content. The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.) Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform. In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in. COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent. TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing. Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users. Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again. Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies. An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform." In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively." Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

coreStoryFacts.text: Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.
TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court.
The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR .
The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”
Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.
PT: The article was updated to include a statement from TikTok.
TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company initially declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.

The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.
Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity. They also flagged that minors were exploiting loopholes to access age-restricted content and hide their activity from parents.
Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”

The statement continues, “We have invested billions of dollars in Trust & Safety and rolled out more than 50 preset safety, privacy, and security settings for teens, including Family Pairing, which helps parents and guardians customize the experience for their teens. We remain steadfast in our commitment to the well-being of our community.”

TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court. The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.

TikTok has reached settlements in several of these cases before they went to trial, including one in Los Angeles where a jury found that Meta and YouTube had designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

sources.title: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act - NPR
passages: TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company initially declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.
It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

After publication, TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown sent a statement saying the citations and claims in the story are "clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works."

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.

Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.)
They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony.
Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.
TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing.

Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time. In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough." Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the court filings. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption "Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague. In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings. The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules. Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K. "If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut." Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law. Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering. If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena. In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions. TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices. The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content. The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit. Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content. The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.) Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform. In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in. COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent. TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing. Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users. Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again. Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies. An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform." In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively." Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

story.title: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act

facts.text: Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.
TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court.
The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR .
The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”
Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.
PT: The article was updated to include a statement from TikTok.
TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company initially declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.
It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

After publication, TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown sent a statement saying the citations and claims in the story are "clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works."

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.

Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.)
They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony.
Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.
TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing.
