extraction.body: As Washington strives for technological dominance and Beijing builds technological self-sufficiency, the global technology system is splitting. The race for technological superiority between the United States and China requires third countries to sustain the advantages of each great power. Europe has a key role to play in this geopolitical rivalry, but its perceptions and cost-benefit analyses are being reevaluated as the Trump administration’s stance toward the European Union becomes more aggressive. Initiatives to build Europe’s technological sovereignty have proliferated in recent years, and opposition to reliance on U.S. platforms has grown as the United States’ retaliatory and punitive measures have intensified. The costs for Europe of building its own technology stack are considerable, with estimates starting at €3.6 trillion . But the security costs of continued reliance on U.S. technology are equally severe. The United States, for its part, is committed to achieving technological dominance . The Trump Administration’s “AI Action Plan” states that the United States “must meet global demand for AI by exporting its full AI technology stack . . . to all countries willing to join America’s AI alliance.” Yet adversarial measures toward longstanding allies, including Europe and Canada, are pushing those same partners to diversify away from U.S. technology, ultimately undermining Washington’s technological ambitions. U.S. technological dominance must be global, and for it to succeed, it must be coproduced. The United States needs allies to not only absorb its technology but also to help produce the technology––all the more so as technological competition concentrates at the cutting edge. Adversarial behaviors and policies, by contrast, will produce the opposite effect, reducing the incentives to rely on U.S. technology and spurring technological indigenization as well as diversification, including toward China. The United States holds a technologically dominant position relative to Europe. Sensitive European government, health, and corporate data is stored on servers subject to U.S. surveillance laws, such as the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data (CLOUD) Act and the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act . Regulatory control over platforms gives the United States the capacity to retaliate against European policy initiatives it perceives as discriminatory. Cloud access can be deliberately interrupted for political purposes. Europe’s perceptions of U.S. hostility are turning these concerns into a conviction that reliance on U.S. technology poses an existential threat. European governments are actively working to move away from U.S. technology. The Tech Sovereignty Package introduced earlier this year, the Cloud and AI Development Act , and the Chips Act 2.0 are emblematic of this shift. France, meanwhile, has restricted the use of Zoom and Microsoft Teams. France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy have joined forces to build European digital commons . Most commentary on these initiatives has questioned their credibility and feasibility. Indeed, in October 2026, Europe-based search engine Ecosia announced it would drop French AI company Mistral from its backend, instead opting to use cheaper and more capable Chinese alternatives. But Europe’s motivation, and the resources it commits to reducing its dependence on U.S. technology, will grow in proportion to perceived U.S. antagonism. While budget strains might complicate these efforts, if national security is on the line, traditional fiscal orthodoxy is still likely to bend, with efforts to decouple increasing at either the supranational or national level. And while Europeans will undergo a costly process of adjustment, Americans risk losing significant market access that will not automatically be absorbed elsewhere. The result will be a net loss on both sides of the Atlantic. The scale of the transatlantic market is far from negligible. In 2025, U.S.-EU trade was valued at approximately $2 trillion . No other bilateral trade and investment relationship in the world is comparable. The transatlantic economy accounts for almost a third of global trade in goods and services and 43 percent of global GDP . Moreover, the relationship is complementary: In 2025, U.S. goods exports to the European Union totaled $412.5 billion and imports $632.9 billion; in services, U.S. exports amounted to $324.8 billion and imports from the bloc to $217.6 billion. In digital services, Europe is a vital market for U.S. cloud providers. In 2025, the market share of U.S. cloud providers in Europe exceeded 80 percent, compared with around 15 percent for European providers. In artificial intelligence, European model providers struggle to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. Dependencies cut both ways: Europe’s reliance on the United States for technology supplies is mirrored by U.S. tech providers’ reliance on European demand. Moreover, U.S. technology is coproduced with European industry leaders. The case is clearest when it comes to U.S. reliance on Dutch company ASML ’s extreme ultraviolet machines. But ASML is not the only U.S. dependency. ZEISS’s optics and TRUMPF’s lasers are indispensable components of the extreme ultraviolet lithography ecosystem; Imec is a critical hub for advanced semiconductor research and development; Ericsson and Nokia are major suppliers of US 5G and telecommunications infrastructure; and companies such as Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Siemens, and Bosch Rexroth are deeply embedded in U.S. automotive, power-electronics, industrial-automation, AI, and manufacturing supply chains. Concerns about U.S. technology affect European businesses as well as governments. EU-listed companies rely on the United States for almost a fifth of their revenues . Yet partnerships with U.S. counterparts and the use of components and technologies with U.S. content expose private companies to the risk of suddenly being targeted by extraterritorial rules. This creates an unfavorable business environment and dims prospects for profitability, motivating supply chain and market diversification. In a 2025 survey, more German companies said they planned to reduce their investments in the United States than said they planned to increase them. Smaller member states have noted that some prospective first-time investors in the United States have abandoned their plans, while businesses with long-standing U.S. relationships planned to continue to invest. Notably, U.S. policies that make alignment with Washington strategically more costly increase the relative attractiveness of diversification. Since Europe began exploring its options in earnest at the start of the second Trump administration, French President Emmanuel Macron made a state visit to China (widely hailed as a success ), with Chinese President Xi Jinping embracing Europe’s aspirations for strategic autonomy. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s also made a trip to China, accompanied by a delegation of business leaders from Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes, and Siemens, all of whom were seeking contracts. The visit’s objective was to “improve and make fair” Sino-German relations. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney––now in the process of formalizing its association partnership with the European Union––also traveled to China earlier this year to forge a “new strategic partnership with People’s Republic of China.” Given Western concerns over Beijing’s trade practices, such visits send a particularly strong signal to Washington : Traditional allies are willing to hedge their technological dependencies for greater economic security. There is still an opportunity to make the transatlantic relationship the foundation of a larger and more resilient technology ecosystem. Restoring the partnership, however, does not mean restoring the status quo. The future transatlantic technology relationship should rather enable both sides to gain control over sensitive technological bottlenecks, thereby restoring a domestic sense of security, while deepening interdependence in areas where capabilities are difficult to develop domestically or are not critical enough to justify the effort. The United States should encourage greater European participation in the U.S. technology ecosystem, including through government procurement, defense cooperation, and commercial partnerships. Precedents for this model already exist: European defense-tech and telecom companies have secured direct U.S. government contracts and entered into transatlantic teaming arrangements. At the same time, Washington should help foster a positive environment for U.S. firms to participate in EU markets and supply chains. There is an appetite for this. Commenting on Intel’s continued partnership with ASML, Intel’s executive vice president said the company “will continue to work closely with ASML and the entire industry to enable [the AI] transition.” In summer 2026, Paris-based Mistral AI established a strategic cloud distribution and infrastructure partnership with Microsoft, allowing European-developed models to run on U.S. hyperscale computing infrastructure. This is notable, considering the company has long been regarded as Europe’s only AI champion. Such deals, however, will multiply only to the extent that governments and companies on both sides of the Atlantic perceive the business climate as positive. Efforts to renew the partnership should not assume that current tensions will simply disappear. A significant segment of European political opinion hopes that the current period of confrontation will pass, much as the relationship recovered after the first Trump administration. Still, U.S. rapprochement will possibly be met with European resentment: European governments might use recent episodes of U.S. aversion as leverage to extract political advantages from future engagement with the United States. While policies adopted today to reduce dependence on the United States could be softened in a period of rapprochement, however, they may still become embedded in Europe’s emerging industrial policy. History points this direction: France’s departure from NATO’s integrated command in 1966 did not end the alliance, but the defense-industrial and nuclear autonomy France built in those years outlasted the rupture by decades. The more plausible outcome, then, is that cooperation will resume on terms that preserve space for European autonomy. If the United States wants Europe to remain part of a U.S.-led technological ecosystem, it needs to make participation the more attractive option for European governments. The United States cannot compete with China while losing its allies. Meeting the China challenge requires building an ecosystem capable of achieving the same scale and offering countries around the world a credible alternative. Europe is indispensable to that effort. Its markets and industrial capabilities sustain the attractiveness and resilience of U.S. technology and enable the United States to shape the next generation of technology. For the United States to win the technology race and establish technological dominance vis-à-vis China, it must first make sure its allies remain in the race with it. This would require Washington to move away from leveraging Europe’s technological dependencies and toward offering Europe a stake in coproducing the technologies of the future, through more open procurement, joint investment, and commitments capable of enduring across administrations. extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13. Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors. Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors. Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders. More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.
Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025.
The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action.
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley pulled off one of the most improbable primary election night comebacks in Wisconsin political history.

This week on Open Record, FOX6's Carl Deffenbaugh, Bryan Polcyn and Jason Calvi are joined by political strategists Joe Zepecki (Democratic) and Bill McCoshen (Republican) to break down his razor's edge win over State Rep.
They also look ahead to his November match up with Republican nominee Tom Tiffany.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Limiting access to AI chatbot apps for children under 13. Prohibiting addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay, on accounts of minors. Increasing penalties for circulating AI-generated sexual images of minors. Allowing families to sue AI platforms if their content harms children, such as by promoting suicide or eating disorders. More funding for adult protective services and resource centers that can help victims of scams or fraud. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. They echo recent bipartisan efforts signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health. extraction.body: NEW YORK — The NFL will have "heightened" security measures around the Saints-Steelers game scheduled to be played Sunday in Paris amid the civil unrest and violence occurring in France, a top league executive said Tuesday. "Our team's been on the ground," said Peter O'Reilly, the NFL's executive vice president of club business, international, and league events. "Our security team's been on the ground and obviously working in close partnership with Stade de France, which is a world-class stadium, hosted world-class events. … But not just on game day. Paris Saint-Germain played Barcelona in a Champions League match Tuesday without incident. The soccer club plays at Parc des Princes, closer to the urban core, while the NFL game will be at the Stade de France in suburban Saint-Dennis. At least seven Saints players were at the soccer game Tuesday. "All of our events we have going on … we always have a very strong security presence, as you know, around all of those events," O'Reilly said. "And that presence will be heightened, with local authorities making sure that there's nothing more important from our standpoint that team security, fan security, everybody involved with this game. So extremely vigilant, as we always are. But, as I said, confident in all of those plans as we head toward Sunday." O'Reilly spoke at a news conference on the opening day of a two-day meeting of the NFL's team owners at a Manhattan hotel. "All of our plans for the Paris game this weekend are moving forward as planned," he said. "We're confident in our operational and security plans. Our team's been on the ground there for about 10 days." The NFL has not given serious consideration to moving or postponing the game, O'Reilly said. "We have never been close to that point," he said. The NFL will vigorously defend its suspensions of two game officials imposed this month for on-field incidents involving players , the league's top football executive said Tuesday. The NFL Referees Association said earlier this month that it would contest those suspensions . The NFLRA called the league's suspensions of line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one game "excessive and inconsistent with past precedent." But Troy Vincent, the NFL's executive vice president of football operations, said Tuesday: "We deal with the consequence of the grievance. We're going to fight that to the very end. And we feel like we resolved it. It's hey, they sat. Adrian returned back this week. Jeff's still out. But those are: You crossed the line. So that's really, frankly, a non-negotiable." Seeman was involved in a verbal exchange with Cardinals tight end Trey McBride following a fourth-quarter play during an Arizona game against the Giants at MetLife Stadium. McBride was on the sideline when Seeman was caught on camera appearing to curse at the tight end. Officials did not call a penalty on a Giants defender on the play. It was not clear what McBride said to Seeman. During a Dolphins-Vikings game, Hill gestured and appeared to yell at Minnesota linebacker Eric Wilson after being knocked to the ground by Wilson on a play that was whistled dead because of a penalty. Wilson was being blocked by a Miami player, and his contact with Hill appeared inadvertent. "That's just unacceptable," Vincent said Tuesday. extraction.body: NEW YORK — The NFL will have "heightened" security measures around the Saints-Steelers game scheduled to be played Sunday in Paris amid the civil unrest and violence occurring in France, a top league executive said Tuesday. "Our team's been on the ground," said Peter O'Reilly, the NFL's executive vice president of club business, international, and league events. "Our security team's been on the ground and obviously working in close partnership with Stade de France, which is a world-class stadium, hosted world-class events. … But not just on game day. Paris Saint-Germain played Barcelona in a Champions League match Tuesday without incident. The soccer club plays at Parc des Princes, closer to the urban core, while the NFL game will be at the Stade de France in suburban Saint-Dennis. At least seven Saints players were at the soccer game Tuesday. "All of our events we have going on … we always have a very strong security presence, as you know, around all of those events," O'Reilly said. "And that presence will be heightened, with local authorities making sure that there's nothing more important from our standpoint that team security, fan security, everybody involved with this game. So extremely vigilant, as we always are. But, as I said, confident in all of those plans as we head toward Sunday." O'Reilly spoke at a news conference on the opening day of a two-day meeting of the NFL's team owners at a Manhattan hotel. "All of our plans for the Paris game this weekend are moving forward as planned," he said. "We're confident in our operational and security plans. Our team's been on the ground there for about 10 days." The NFL has not given serious consideration to moving or postponing the game, O'Reilly said. "We have never been close to that point," he said. The NFL will vigorously defend its suspensions of two game officials imposed this month for on-field incidents involving players , the league's top football executive said Tuesday. The NFL Referees Association said earlier this month that it would contest those suspensions . The NFLRA called the league's suspensions of line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one game "excessive and inconsistent with past precedent." But Troy Vincent, the NFL's executive vice president of football operations, said Tuesday: "We deal with the consequence of the grievance. We're going to fight that to the very end. And we feel like we resolved it. It's hey, they sat. Adrian returned back this week. Jeff's still out. But those are: You crossed the line. So that's really, frankly, a non-negotiable." Seeman was involved in a verbal exchange with Cardinals tight end Trey McBride following a fourth-quarter play during an Arizona game against the Giants at MetLife Stadium. McBride was on the sideline when Seeman was caught on camera appearing to curse at the tight end. Officials did not call a penalty on a Giants defender on the play. It was not clear what McBride said to Seeman. During a Dolphins-Vikings game, Hill gestured and appeared to yell at Minnesota linebacker Eric Wilson after being knocked to the ground by Wilson on a play that was whistled dead because of a penalty. Wilson was being blocked by a Miami player, and his contact with Hill appeared inadvertent. "That's just unacceptable," Vincent said Tuesday. extraction.body: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source.
“I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.”

Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers.

The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.

(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term capital market assumptions for the first time, forecasting returns that could beat stocks, bonds and gold in a milestone for its Wall Street acceptance.
The firm stops short of incorporating Bitcoin into its main portfolio models, it said in a report this week, citing its unstable correlations with other assets.

The JPMorgan analysts say that even as many investors see Bitcoin as a speculative asset, they're still exploring cryptocurrencies — a tenth of clients recently surveyed said their portfolios held crypto, and roughly 17% said they planned to "prioritize crypto." That's thanks, in part, to a regulatory framework that has become more developed and better defined.
But there's a catch: Bitcoin's extreme volatility threatens to undermine its appeal on a risk-adjusted basis.

(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term capital market assumptions for the first time, forecasting returns that could beat stocks, bonds and gold in a milestone for its Wall Street acceptance.
The firm stops short of incorporating Bitcoin into its main portfolio models, it said in a report this week, citing its unstable correlations with other assets.

But there's a catch: Bitcoin's extreme volatility threatens to undermine its appeal on a risk-adjusted basis.

JPMorgan's base case projects annualized returns of 10% over the next decade, but also assumes annual volatility of 55%, more than three times that of US large-cap stocks. The firm stops short of incorporating Bitcoin into its main portfolio models, it said in a report this week, citing its unstable correlations with other assets.

Such volatility can eat into compounded returns as steep losses require even larger gains to recover. That's a risk familiar to Bitcoin ETF investors who bought near the cryptocurrency's peak of just over $126,000 in 2025, only to see their holdings lose as much as 50% as prices retreated.

"We believe it is premature to consider BTC as a diversifier in a balanced portfolio," the JPMorgan team including Tim Lintern, Thushka Maharaj and Sean Daly wrote. "But should volatility continue to decline and correlations to other asset stabilize, this may evolve in the future, particularly as regulation becomes clearer and liquidity and price discovery continue to improve."

Since the pandemic, various Wall Street firms have been making more earnest inroads into the world of cryptocurrencies, shifting from cautious inquiry to more meaningful experimentation that's included making the trading of certain coins available for clients, putting out crypto-focused funds and dabbling with tokenization, among other things.

The JPMorgan analysts say that even as many investors see Bitcoin as a speculative asset, they're still exploring cryptocurrencies — a tenth of clients recently surveyed said their portfolios held crypto, and roughly 17% said they planned to "prioritize crypto." That's thanks, in part, to a regulatory framework that has become more developed and better defined.

Still, Bitcoin right now doesn't cut it as a diversifier in balance portfolios due to its "unstable correlations" to other assets, the bank's researchers said. "If correlations stabilize and volatility declines, BTC's portfolio utility may improve in the future," they wrote.

More broadly, the researchers in their note explored how "economic nationalism, technology adoption and capital rewiring" could drive asset returns over the next decade or so, coming to the conclusion that governments will invest in "national resiliency," firms will race to deploy new innovations and those factors will impact how capital gets deployed. A $15 trillion "global capex supernova" will fuel growth and strong asset returns over the period, they said.

"Technology adoption today is synonymous with artificial intelligence, but breakthroughs in other areas, from medicine to robotics to space, will likely advance in the next decade, further supporting trend growth via investment and productivity," the report stated.

Banks that impose transfer limits received 6,198 complaints, while those without a published policy restricting crypto transfers received 2,842.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY) received the most complaints, at 2,297, followed by Barclays (LON: BARC) with 1,569 and NatWest Group (LON: NWG) with 1,278.
Lloyds, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, accounted for more than 22% of the total complaints.
The complaints involved all major UK retail banks and came from every one of the country's 650 parliamentary constituencies.
HSBC UK (LSE: HSBA) and Monzo were also among the banks named in the report, which found that restrictions were not limited to institutions with explicit crypto bans.

Stand With Crypto said the figures suggest customers cannot reliably predict whether their bank will allow them to transfer money to regulated crypto platforms, even when the bank does not publicly prohibit such payments.

sources.title: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys - Decrypt
passages: Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

extraction.body: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards. Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.” The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections. Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit. Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.” The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022. Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 . In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account. Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card. This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money. “If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.” However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account. “And that happens more often than you might think," he adds. Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively. Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved. passages: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys
Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

sources.title: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys - Decrypt
passages: Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.” The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections. Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit. Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.” The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022. Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 . In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account. Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card. This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money. “If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.” However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account. “And that happens more often than you might think," he adds. Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively. Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved. "Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.” Start every day with the top news stories right now, plus original features, a podcast, videos and more. © 2026 Decrypt Media, Inc. extraction.body: Alaska’s effort to appease President Trump’s claims that noncitizens are voting has ended up punishing U.S. citizens. The Alaska Beacon reported Thursday that the state removed 3,048 people from its active voter list, including many citizens who were accidentally flagged by the Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles and now have to provide extra identification to be able to vote. The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, Carol Beecher, told state legislators on Wednesday that “old data” was the reason for the mistake and that she wasn’t sure why so many Alaska residents were labeled as noncitizens. When Alaskans apply for a driver’s license, they are asked whether they want to register to vote and if they are a U.S. citizen. State election officials cross-check the DMV’s records with voter rolls each year, and according to Beecher, “more like 200 names” are typically tagged for extra scrutiny. The latest check found “a lot more names than we were expecting,” Beecher said. “We believe that when we did the match, that a lot of old data was picked up somehow. So we’re still ferreting through that,” Beecher said, adding that although the number of flagged names was “very concerning,” the state has to take them seriously. “It is not disenfranchising the individual from being able to vote, but it’s a measure the division has to take to make sure that we only have citizens voting.” Beecher said that those who were flagged will receive a letter asking if they are citizens, and that they merely need to contact the state Division of Elections by email, phone, or regular mail, and state they are a citizen. “We don’t require paperwork. We’re not requiring documentation. Nothing like that,” she added. Eligible U.S. citizens who were removed from the voter rolls disagree. Chris Waigl, who got her driver’s license in 2019 and became a U.S. citizen in 2025, was alarmed to check her registration status last weekend and find that she was listed as “inactive—non citizen.” “They were able to correct it there and then after I sent in copies of my naturalization certificate with a date before my voter registration date,” she told the Beacon via email. “It’s just ridiculous.” Waigl said she reached out to four others who became citizens at the same time as her, and three of them were removed from the voter rolls. One of them told the Beacon by phone that they were removed despite registering in person at a DMV office and presenting citizenship information. Some people told the Beacon that they haven’t been able to reach the Division of Elections by phone, and that mailboxes are full. Alaska’s primary elections are less than a month away on August 18, and the general election is less than two months away in November. The state’s lieutenant governor, Nancy Dahlstrom, is in charge of the elections office and has told state officials to comply with the Trump administration’s requests to turn over copies of Alaska’s voter rolls for a national voter database. But that national database, run by the Department of Homeland Security, has been found to be full of errors , mistakenly flagging U.S. citizens. One month ago, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan struck it down, saying that the government “haphazardly” created a database of millions of Americans it knew was “inaccurate.” “States have partnered with the federal government to access the database and are actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information,” Soonam wrote in a 75-page ruling . “All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote.” Between the Trump administration and zealous state governments like Alaska’s, thousands of U.S. citizens may not be able to vote in this year’s midterms. President Donald Trump is suddenly reneging on the terms of the Gordie Howe Bridge project after he claimed Ottawa “disinvited” U.S. officials from the Michigan–Ontario crossing’s grand opening. “Canada disinvited the United States of America to the opening of the Gordie Howe Bridge, which is fine, considering they are paying substantial TARIFFS to the United States, but the original Deal on the Bridge, which was terribly negotiated by a previous Administration, no longer stands,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday. “We changed the terms of the Deal so that the United States of America now gets 50 percent of the Profit.” The Gordie Howe Bridge was the creation of a very different period in U.S.-Canadian relations. The international bridge was first proposed in the early 2000s and agreed upon by the two nations in 2012. Under the terms of that agreement, Canada would fully pay for the bridge to get the project moving forward and only share toll revenue once it had recovered its initial costs. At the time, President Barack Obama was revered by America’s northern neighbors, and diplomatic relations between the two countries were good. But Trump has worked hard to undo that long-standing goodwill. Over the last year and a half, the U.S. president has repeatedly attacked Canada, punishing its people with enormous tariffs, baselessly accosting its government, and even threatening to invade its land to make another U.S. state. The latest insult came earlier this week, when Trump announced 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products worth $20 billion. Canada rescinded its invitations to U.S. officials for the bridge’s grand opening ceremony shortly thereafter, and moved the ribbon-cutting ceremony from the international border line at the center of the bridge to a nearby inspection plaza. “In light of trade action threatened by the United States earlier this week, it would be inappropriate to proceed with a celebratory event between the two countries,” the office of Canada’s infrastructure minister said, in a statement obtained by The New York Times . “The Gordie Howe International Bridge remains a vital infrastructure project that reflects years of hard work and will be a major economic driver.” Now Trump is threatening the bridge by claiming that the two countries will split the revenue 50-50, which was not what was agreed upon nearly 15 years ago. Americans have little, if any, confidence that government officials like Kennedy are up to the task of solving these public health crises. With all of the budget cuts to government regulators, the U.S. probably hasn’t seen the last disease outbreak of Trump’s presidency. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is literally running away from accusations of voter fraud. A bombshell report earlier this month exposed Paxton for allegedly voting in six elections while registered at an address where he does not live. On Friday, while entering the Ronald Reagan Republican Center in Washington, D.C., Paxton was asked point-blank whether he had committed voter fraud. Rather than face the music, the attorney general raced inside. Q: Mr Paxton, did you commit voter fraud? KEN PAXTON: *walks away* (This is at least the third time just this week he's literally run away from questions of this sort) pic.twitter.com/HZWvR9w1y5 This isn’t the first time Paxton has run from questions about his alleged voter fraud. Earlier this week, Paxton fled a press conference when faced with tough questions, earning him the nickname “ No Comment Ken .” “This is at least the third time just this week he’s literally run away from questions of this sort,” journalist Aaron Rupar wrote on X. In another tough moment on Thursday, Paxton refused to answer whether he was ready to debate James Talarico, the Democratic Texas Senate candidate, who has publicly accused his opponent of voter fraud. This form of voter fraud is a second-degree felony punishable by a fine up to $10,000 and up to 20 years in prison. While stopping short of referring to Weiss by name, Vega said her decision to tell the story strictly through the eyes of West Virginians had spurred backlash from CBS’s “new” top brass because she had not interviewed Vice President JD Vance or referred to his decade-old memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.
But Vance, as Vega pointed out, is from Ohio. Not West Virginia.

passages: Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown , take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate.
He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.
They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned.
So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them.
They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices.
LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given.
The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize.
The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.
The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm.
The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do.

It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”
But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices.

extraction.body: Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown , take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents. “Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.” To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well , including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened. In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible. But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack. In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.” Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.” But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers. The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack. But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote. It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen. Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!” In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.

“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”

To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well , including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.

In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”

Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”

But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.

But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.

It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen.
Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”
In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

The architecture addresses the fundamental identity gap in multi-agent AI systems through four complementary mechanisms:
Deepakkumar is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services specializing in generative AI, security architecture, and cloud-native application design.
He works with enterprise customers to build secure AI systems on AWS and is passionate about bringing cryptographic identity to the AI agent ecosystem.

The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation.
While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials.
You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments.
When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement.
The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user.
Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand.
EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation.
EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).
The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms.
First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call.
Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials.
Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure.
Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents.
As AI agents proliferate and gain access to increasingly sensitive operations, agent identity infrastructure moves from optional to essential.
This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization.
The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK .

When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization. In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK . While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments. The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table. Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup. The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution. The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token. First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization. Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll REST API endpoint. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role. Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate. When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with RSA-PSS-SHA256 . The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate. Sub-agents cannot call each other, can’t call upward to the orchestrator, and cannot impersonate the user. The PKI architecture provides built-in behavior boundaries for the AI agents in this system. Production deployments should use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering, topic avoidance, and grounding checks on agent responses, alongside the PKI-based access controls described in this post. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments. The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token. First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization. Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role. Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate.
